quoted_text:
: : [Institution/Report] Beyond the Dollar: The Conditions for Sovereign Debt Tokenization, and Why Korea Is the First Clean Test
Written by Sam Shim (Meritz Securities), Data supported by @100y_eth 

- Tokenized US Treasuries reached about 15.9 billion dollars in July 2026, and technology was only part of it. The dollar market had supplied a fund structure institutions were allowed to hold, demand that existed before the first token, and recurring fee income.

- Token standards, custody, and settlement are now available off the shelf, so infrastructure is no longer the constraint. Products outside the dollar are still under a tenth of tokenized government debt, and that number measures what has been built rather than what investors want.

- Demand starts with stablecoin reserves, because a coin wants its backing in its own currency and onchain. Only a tokenized government bond in that currency is both, which makes reserves the only demand proven so far, while collateral and diversification have not appeared yet.

- Korea has most of what that demand sequence needs in one market, and foreign investors can already buy its bonds. Bond sourcing and won conversion run through domestic infrastructure, and a won stablecoin already holds a tokenized Korean government bond in reserve, though only at symbolic size.

- The whole argument rests on one bet, that what is missing is the product, not the appetite. The strongest objection is that onchain capital structurally prefers the dollar, and the report sets out the evidence that would settle it stage by stage.

Full Report:
https://t.co/22IZiY0rgN

text:
AI越来越聪明，但一个问题也越来越重要：

AI给的数据，凭什么是真的？
AI替你执行交易，又凭什么保证没出错？

研究了下 DeepSafe，我觉得它做的事情可以用一句大白话概括：

给 Web2、Web3 和 AI 加一个“验真层”。

传统方案很多时候依赖固定的 Oracle、节点或多签参与方，一旦数据被篡改、节点被攻击甚至发生合谋，安全性就会下降。

DeepSafe 的核心 CRVA，则希望通过随机选择验证节点、隐藏节点身份、多人共同签名以及动态轮换，把“相信某个人或机构”，变成“验证密码学证明”。

它能延伸的场景也比较多：
AI Agent 输入输出、Oracle 数据、跨链消息、钱包资产操作，以及链上链下数据验证等。

这也是我比较关注 DeepSafe 的原因。

未来 AI Agent 如果真的开始帮人交易、跨链甚至管理资产，AI越强，验证AI有没有拿错数据、做错事情反而越重要。

所以 DeepSafe 押注的，本质上不是单一产品，而是一个长期需求：

AI负责做事，区块链负责结算，DeepSafe这类验证网络负责证明——这件事到底是不是真的、有没有按规则执行。

AI时代不缺聪明的机器。

真正稀缺的，可能是证明机器没有骗你的能力。

这个方向现在还比较早，但逻辑我觉得值得研究。
如果未来AI真的开始替你管钱，你敢不加一道验证，就把资产权限直接交给它吗？

quoted_text:
Meta may use Phoenix at next week’s Connect to demo full-body, photorealistic hologram calls, with Boz appearing as a hologram.

Let me start with this. Meta’s Codec Avatars and Apple’s Personas are incredible technologies. They are solving something that would have been hard to imagine not long ago. Turning a real person, including their face, expressions, gaze and movements, into a live 3D presence.

But incredible technology does not necessarily mean the final product will be one lifelike avatar for each person.

I have two questions.

1.  How many avatars will each person have in the future? One, a hundred, or a thousand?

I think we will have many. We will change avatars like we change clothes, depending on the setting, our mood and the stage of life we are in. It may go much further than clothing. We could use entirely different bodies for work, meeting friends, attending concerts and playing games.

VRChat already gives paid users 250 extra favorite avatar slots.

2.  How many of these avatars will actually look like our real selves?

An avatar does not have to be an exact copy of me, or simply a better-looking version of me. It may be the version of myself I want to express at a particular moment and in a particular setting.

That answer will be different for everyone. Some people will want to resemble their real selves. Others will want to become something completely different. Many may not even want to appear human. Age, gender, body and even species could all become choices.

So I think the greatest value of Codec Avatars is that they create a technological foundation for avatars. They can capture a person’s expressions, gaze, movements and presence, then use them to animate many different forms.

The real self is the input. The avatar is the expression.

‼️ BREAKING: Our investigations team at Duel is in contact with the Revolut hacker, and we've found out a lot more about how he did what he did.

- The hacker got access to government employee accounts using an infostealer. After gaining access to an employee's email, they would log in, add their own recovery email, start to log everything, and silently listen in.

- To not get caught, they would instantly delete any email sent that was not intended for the original employee. The inbox was checked 24/7 for any new response to the hacker's sent emails. Upon receiving one, the hacker would instantly download it as a .eml and delete it before the original employee noticed

- The hacker says that at first he used to forge court orders (presumably when targeting other companies), but quickly realised that this wouldn't work for Revolut. After some research, they decided the best entity to target was Revolut's Lithuania-based Revolut Bank UAB, which would respond to a European Investigation Order (as shown in the images).

- With this stolen email, the hacker sent one request, originally 5 months ago, attached below. Revolut believed it, thinking it was the Italian government, and complied with the order.

- From the hacked email, the hacker was able to control and end emails that looked like they genuinely came from multiple Italian government email addresses.

- The hacker continuously sent out requests over the course of 5 months. Not once did Revolut ask questions or not send over the information. In one incident, the hacker accidentally sent the wrong document. Instead of realising what was going on, Revolut's support guided them on what to change (shown in an image below)

We remain in contact with the hacker and we've requested exclusivity of information related to the story to be kept with Duel. We believe it is in the public's best interest for EVERY piece of information related to this to be released, so that the extent of Revolut's failure can be brought to light, as well as the sheer stupidity of the manner in which the KYC paradigm is currently conducted.

The Duel team hopes that Revolut will be held accountable for their lack of due diligence and betraying their customers in such a severe manner, especially given the breadth and depth of the breach. Lives are now at risk. I'm personal friends with one of the victims, and he'll probably have to move houses due to the continued (credible) kidnap threats.

We hope to soon release a much more detailed article with more information, emails, screenshots and more.

text:
Crazy… 

Odyssey just released Odyssey-3, a foundation world model that can work with very different bodies, from humanoids and robot arms to cars, drones and even virtual characters.

What’s interesting is how they’re building it. Instead of training a separate model for every robot, Odyssey first trains one model to understand how the world works: how things move, how people behave, and how actions change the environment. Then you only need a relatively small amount of data to teach it how to operate a new body. Their driving model, for example, was trained with just 20 hours of simulated driving data.

So the model doesn’t have to learn everything again every time it gets a new body. It already has some understanding of the world; the new data mainly teaches it how to use that particular body.

---
TBH,this is starting to feel a little like Rehoboam from Westworld: one intelligence, operating through many different bodies.

Could this be one path toward general-purpose physical AI? https://t.co/UejIircBfh

I'm gonna regret posting this cuz it's our best growth hack and anyone can do it, BUT

here's how to get 500k-10m+ views on your launch video (every time, infinitely repeatable)

its great bc if you do it right, you can make a new vid every few wks and drive crazy inbound. 

We do one a month and consistently clear 250k+ views

1. make a launch video. record it yourself with a screen-capture tool like Screen Studio or get a good freelance editor to put it together for you.

2. start your tweet with a hook that stops the scroll. think "the world's first ___" or "today we're making ___ obsolete."

3. personally, I search for viral X launches from the past two months with Origami's content mode and look for formats I can reuse (they've already performed well, so you're not starting from zero)

4. once you find those massive launches (10m+ views), study the opening line, video structure, and quote tweets that got traction. use those patterns when you launch.

5. message your network (investors, friends, former coworkers). tell them exactly what day and time you're going live.

6. when the post is live, email everyone who said they'd help. include the launch tweet and a clear explanation of what you're asking them to do.

7. spell out the main message and include a few example quote tweets they can adapt in their own words. (follow X's rules on disclosed posts)

8. ask everyone to engage within the first hour if they're around.

9. you can also put paid spend behind the video after a day or two to give it another push.

10. launch again whenever you ship a major feature that could stand on its own as a product.
--------------

the best part is if it flops, barely anyone saw it anyway.

so change the hook and try again the following week. people literally "launch" 3-5 times a month and it works

would love to see more great launch videos on X

I'll be sharing more growth playbooks here every week

author: SingularityNET
quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

text:
Day 15: 
Hertzflow 100$  Survival Challenge.
The challenge has ended. However, I still want to share some of my experiences throughout the challenge.
* First: thanks to @Hertzflow_xyz for organizing the challenge and providing the initial capital. It was a fair campaign, with everyone starting with the same capital and the same amount of time.
My goal wasn't just to make the Top 10, even though I ultimately didn't make it. 
But also to join the project early, experience HertzFlow firsthand, and maximize my trading volume during the challenge. 
* I think I made nearly 150 trades throughout the challenge, and I’m still going.
1:  Start with one simple rule.
- With $100, protecting the account matters more than chasing profits.
- I avoided oversized positions and focused on manageable setups.
- One bad trade shouldn't end the challenge.
2: My trading approach.
- Mainly focused on short-term trades.
- Followed BTC, ETH, BNB and XAU.
- Waited for setups instead of trying to predict the market.
- I made nearly 150 trades. More trades created more opportunities and volume, but not every trade was a good one.
- Some losses taught me the most. One trade hit nearly +27%, but I didn't take profit and eventually got stopped out.
- I also FOMO'd into CPI and lost around 50% of my challenge account.
3: Final Lesson.
- Profit → Survival → Learning.
- The challenge wasn't about making the most trades, but staying in the game long enough to learn.
- 150 trades gave me a lot of real trading experience, but the losing trades taught me more than the winning ones.
4: A Few Things about HertzFlow.
- These 14 days gave me the chance to experience HertzFlow more closely.
- One thing I like about HertzFlow is that you can connect your wallet and keep control of your assets while trading, without depositing them into a centralized exchange.
- I like its simple, streamlined, and easy-to-use interface. Flexible leverage of up to 95x.
- Currently, HertzFlow supports BTC, ETH, BNB, and XAU. I hope to see more trading pairs added in the future.
-  Another thing I'd like HertzFlow to improve is the trading fees, as lower fees would make frequent trading more attractive.
* The challenge was a great experience. I learned a lot, made mistakes, and had the opportunity to experience HertzFlow through real trading.
* Once again, thanks to the HertzFlow team for organizing the challenge and giving me the opportunity to participate. Looking forward to what comes next.
* This is based on my personal experience and is not financial or investment advice.

In our last competition, Cacheon miners pushed MiniMax M3 throughput to 2,337.9 tok/s: +32.2% vs the SGLang baseline.

What might that kind of performance improvement be worth commercially?

+32.2% throughput = ~61% more profit.

How? SemiAnalysis InferenceX™ models a B300 running MiniMax M3 on vLLM at $4.81 profit per chip-hour. Apply the same +32.2% throughput gain, with pricing and chip costs held constant, and modeled profit rises to $7.73 per chip-hour.

Why the difference? The GPU still costs $4.25 for the hour. More throughput means more capacity to sell without buying another chip-hour.

That's a scenario, not measured Cacheon profit. What is measured is the optimization: 2,337.9 tok/s, +32.2%, produced by Bittensor miners and passed through Cacheon's testing and reproduction.

Check the baseline. Run your own numbers.

text:
The Clarity Act failing today makes everybody a loser, all because partisan jockeying beat out common sense:

The lines between tokens and securities are no more clear.

Entrepreneurs will still prefer to build and raise capital offshore.

Investors will receive no more information, or protections.

Developers have no additional safeguards for decentralized systems.

Banks are stuck with stablecoins able to pay rewards (yield).

There are zero ethical guardrails for government employees and crypto.

The list goes on.

But mostly I just feel for the countless folks in the industry and across the House and Senate (of both parties) that worked on this for so long, and the light of American leadership dimming just a tad.

Onwards

text:
假如将手上的总资金假设为100

比较好的策略是90%是BTC，10%是其他高风险/高回报币种。

这里从数学上简单计算一下：

假如未来是大牛市，比特币翻倍，而小币涨5倍，那么，计算如下：

90 BTC × 2 = 180
10 小币 × 5 = 50

 最终余额为230，收益+130%

而作为最坏的情况下，假设各种利空，BTC真的回去5万之类，那么假设BTC跌30%，小币跌90%，则计算如下：

90 BTC × 0.7 = 63
10 小币 × 0.1 = 1

最终余额为64，亏损36%

那如果全部买BTC，同样两种行情分别是：
牛市：100 → 200
 熊市：100 → 70

这个结果不差，但是对照我的杠铃策略，即只拿10%的本金去承担“跌90%”的风险，整个组合因此多损失9个百分点；但如果它真的抓到5倍-10倍机会，却可以让整个组合收益大大增长。

杠铃策略：大部分资产负责让我们留在牌桌上，小部分资产负责改变投资的斜率。

但如果把比例反过来呢？比如小币拉满呢？最坏的情况下，直接本金只有10块了，那时候，如果后悔了买BTC，需要BTC涨10倍才回本…

10块赚到100块并不容易，但用100块赚另外100块容易得多，选择做容易一点的事，就需要守住本金。

具体参阅图片。最后惯例推荐大家安装使用FOMO，我现在日常操作和发现热币全是用它了。

首要是因为足够安全，这是底线，它作为美国合规项目方，融资了近亿美元，估值高，用户数极短时间到千万量级，采取的无私钥钱包方案，用户的钱在自己掌握，比较放心。

其次是使用方便，不再需要关注什么合约地址，也不用管什么链，直接一键秒买，这一点对资金使用率来说非常重要，临时有个热币不用再去提币和跨链，关键时刻这能赚回一切。另外，上面主流币费率只有币安的一半，加上合约什么都有，真的是除了出入金，我已经不再需要CEX了。

okx wallet:https://t.co/MBLMJafAEB

Launchpad + DEX trading terminal + on-chain intelligence tools.

The official account says the product is positioned as more than just a launchpad. It is designed as a complete discover → chart → trade → manage → launch workflow:

Creator Studio: Launch a token and create its liquidity pool in a single transaction.
Market Atlas / Trade Studio: Market discovery, charts, Quick Buy, and protective orders.
Intelligence Layer: Signal Lens, Holder Map, Opportunity Map, Live Tape, Bubbles.
Portfolio: Holdings, rewards, points, and transfers.
Telegram: Trading and cross-pool aggregation.
Uniswap v4 Hooks: Future support for composable tax rates, dividends, programmable assets, and similar mechanisms.

The biggest difference from Pump is the launch mechanism

There is no bonding curve, no graduation, and no migration.

The process is:A single transaction deploys a fixed-supply token and creates a TOKEN/USDC Uniswap V3 1% pool. The entire supply is placed into single-sided liquidity, while the LP NFT is permanently locked in TollyFeeLocker.

From the first trade, this is already the final market.

The price rises as more USDC is bought along the liquidity range. During the initial launch period, there is a temporary per-wallet holding limit for anti-sniping, which is removed later.

The contract is open-source and has verified bytecode.

Native Tolly market fee structure

The native Tolly market charges a 1% pool fee.

Buy-side allocation:

64% → Creator
12% → Market holder rewards
10% → Protocol treasury
9% → Buyback and removal of TOLLY from circulation
5% → Buyback and removal of the project token

Sell-side:100% → Project token burn
Creator receives no USDC from the sell-side fee
TOLLY

TOLLY is the core token of the platform economy.

For native markets, 9% of the buy-side fee continuously goes toward buying back and burning TOLLY.

On TOLLY’s own market, both the 9% + 5% mechanisms point toward TOLLY, making the buy-side burn particularly strong.

Sell-side fees directly burn the project token, while protocol development fees are also used to buy TOLLY into the strategic reserve for product and ecosystem development.

Simply put:More on-chain trading volume → More buyback & burn + More USDC rewards for holders.

text:
Institutions entering onchain credit changes the product.

“What’s the yield?” becomes:

> who’s the counterparty?
> will compliance sign off?

text:
I did a small experiment. Had something I wanted reviewed properly. My usual options were: read it all myself (it was huge and it would have taken me days), or throw it at one big model (and burn tokens, probably I would have exhausted my limit several times in the process).

So I tried to build a reviewer team. Fable as the orchestrator. It didn't review anything. It spun up a couple of VMs with the jl CLI, wrote one brief per reviewer, kicked them off, and sat there triaging what came back.

The actual reviewing went to GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash which are available on https://t.co/nmbjqEyvYS Models APIs. Four of them, each with a narrow job. One only cared about logic. One only about code quality. One pretended to be the user. One just tried to break it, and all of them ran inside opencode sessions, which gave them hands.

Now every serious finding went to a second model that hadn't seen the first one's reasoning. Reproduce it or it gets rejected. That step alone removed most of the noise.

The Orchestrator used a fraction of the tokens the workers did, and the workers were the cheap ones.

Not sure this generalises to everything. But I want to try this workflow for sometime and see if it makes my life easier. I think the workflow can be improved a lot: the orchestrator could also act as a reviewer across the different models, hold more of the context itself, and be used more effectively. Open to some ideas for the same.

I tried this orchestration with Fable 5.1 and Astra at the same time. Fable figured out what needed to be done faster. Astra got confused, took a lot of time, and frustrated me , so I did not continue with it. (though I used computer use to test later which was amazing).

text:
I was born and raised in a village. I lost both of my parents when I was just 17 years old.

At that age, I never really had the chance to grieve. Life did not give me the luxury of stopping to process the pain. I had to keep moving, keep working, and somehow find a way to survive while carrying a loss I barely understood.
As I grew older, I began to realize something grieving is a privilege. Sometimes, you have to survive first before you can afford to grieve.
But somewhere along that journey, I also discovered that grief can carry purpose. The pain of losing the people who brought you into this world can become a reason to build, to persevere, and to become the person you wish they could have seen.
I didn’t choose the circumstances that shaped me, but I can choose what I do with them.

To anyone grieving ..give yourself time to feel, heal, and remember. You don’t have to be strong every day. Keep going !! your pain can become your strength and your purpose.

🚨NEW @JTLonsdale with @JesseBWatters on what's really behind the AI doomerism: 

"They've given up Christianity in most of San Francisco... if you give up religion, you want some kind of messianic complex, some kind of big thing to believe in.

These effective altruists — this is their Messiah, this is their end of the world, this is their obsession."

Jesse Waters: Am I going wrong anywhere, Joe? 

Joe Lonsdale: I think President Trump and you are correct. There is a coordinated campaign to make the American people afraid... There's over 50 organizations that were coordinating campaigns, doing narrative intelligence tests, testing public opinion, and spending huge amounts of money trying to scare people.

It's regulatory capture, on one hand. It's our adversaries, of course, want us to stop. And I'll tell you what else it is: America has always been very religious, but they've given up Christianity in most of San Francisco. So this is like a messianic complex where this is their religion and the end of the world. And they're obsessed with it. It's weird.

Jesse: So these guys don't believe in God. They're atheists, but they've created something which they believe is god like, is that what's going on here?

Joe: I think that's a big part of what's happening. Listen, AI is real by the way. What you said is right, there's an industrial revolution coming that's amazing for America if we get it right. People who hate America want to stop it. 

But yes, America has always... we were founded by kind of extreme Puritans, right? We've always been very, very religious. We've had these awakenings. 

And I think this is a form of what happens if you give up religion is you want to have some kind of messianic complex, some kind of big thing to believe in. And these effective altruists, this is their Messiah and this is their end of the world and this is their obsession. So I think it is a little bit unhealthy in terms of the spiritual life in San Francisco that's broken.

Jesse: So the chip guy, who runs Nvidia, he's basically saying it's not true. There is no even 10% chance of human extinction from AI. Do you believe that? 

Joe: Yeah, I believe that. I think there's definitely risks where, for example, if the I guess if people use it for viral synthesis and a DNA synthesis site, they could cause a lot of deaths. I think there's going to be lots of hacking that happens thanks to AI being used by people. I think there's other risks that we can't yet understand for how authoritarians could use this... to trick the populace by being really good at knowing how to appeal to huge numbers of people about horrible things.

So there's lots of risks, and there's lots of upside. But I think these doomer narratives are ridiculous. And I think we should be embracing the industrial revolution, and we should be pushing back on these NGOs. By the way, the same thing they did last time with climate change, with killer bees... These guys want power. They want money. We shouldn't buy it.

Jesse: Killer bees. I forgot about that one. So you're saying you could use it to control the population, but, I mean, we could also use it to root out corruption in the federal government. Are Democrats kind of scared that that I could be used against them?

Joe: I think that's exactly right. I think people don't realize how much AI is on the side of liberty, how much is anti-corruption. Scott Bessent's doing a great job as Treasury Secretary and changing the rules so we can look through things, we can start using AI. There's investigative journalists already getting going, finding all sorts of fraud in HHS that only AI could have found because there's so much to look through.

And so, yes, I think it's going to be a very positive thing for society. It's going to root out all that money that they're stealing and moving around to their NGOs, and they don't want that happening. I think you're right about that.

text:
这两天我一直在玩 Project Mars。 

本来只是想小额试一下，现在已经买了两块地，开始每 4 小时烧 900 DRILL 跑一轮 Excavator。

为什么我会越玩越深？

因为它目前看起来，不只是一个“发币—挖矿—卖币”的游戏，而是真的做出了一套链上生产经济。

最简单理解：

买 Plot（土地）
→ 烧 DRILL 开矿机
→ 几小时后随机挖出 DRILL、Ore、Slush
→ Ore 可以升级土地
→ 土地等级越高，Weight 和 Owner Bonus 越高
→ 别人来你的地上挖矿，你作为地主也能拿 Bonus
→ Slush / Ore 还可以进入 Refinery 继续加工

也就是说，DRILL 不只是奖励币。

开矿机会直接 Burn DRILL，升级、建筑、Refinery 又会继续产生资源消耗。

而升级之后，生产能力又会进一步提高。

这也是我愿意真金白银测试它的原因：

它至少已经形成了“消耗 → 生产 → 升级 → 提高生产效率”的闭环。

但有闭环，不代表一定赚钱。

我自己的结果就非常典型。

我先买了两块地：

#3042：0.0795 ETH，L5
#123：0.09 ETH，L10

最开始只用最便宜的 Scout 测了一轮。

后来开始在 #123 跑 T4 Excavator：

每轮成本 900 DRILL，周期 4 小时。

第一轮：

900 DRILL → 1146.98 DRILL

光 DRILL 就 +246.98，还挖到了 Ore 和 Slush。

当时第一感觉：这个效率有点夸张。

结果第二轮马上给我上了一课：

900 DRILL → 694.32 DRILL

光 DRILL -205.68。

把两轮挖出来的 Ore 按当时市场真实可成交的价格算进去，目前整体仍然是正收益。

但很明显：

这不是固定 APR，而是一套高波动的生产系统。

所以我现在还不敢下结论说 Project Mars 能稳定赚钱。

我真正想验证的是：

长期跑矿机，算上 DRILL、Ore、Bonus、gas 后，真实 EV 到底是多少；

买高等级土地当地主，靠其他玩家挖矿产生的 Bonus 和 Plot 收益，能不能形成稳定现金流；

以及 Ore 用来升级土地以后，提高的生产效率到底值不值升级成本。

还有最关键的一件事：

游戏里赚到的东西，最终能不能真正变回 ETH。

因为我现在已经跑到第四轮 T4，另一块地也马上够材料升级了。

地越来越多，矿越来越多，生产能力也越来越强……

但我最近突然发现：

怎么感觉自己一直在挖、一直在升级、一直在复投，真正拿回来的 ETH 却没多少 😂

所以接下来我准备认真把这笔账算清楚：

到底投了多少本金，多久能真正回本，以及回本之后这套系统还能不能持续产生现金流。

如果最后跑通了，它可能不只是一个挖矿小游戏，而是一门挺有意思的链上小生意。

如果跑不通，我也会把真实过程发出来。

https://t.co/KQPRYWke5m

加入我的社群一起研究：
https://t.co/Z5GxfEJkGA

Over those months, @viharkurama and I spent hours with the team debating trade-offs and working from first principles. The hard part was fitting an agent into Plane's foundation and the way a real workspace operates.

We set five requirements:

1/ Follow Plane's permission model, with access limited by workspace roles and the projects you choose.

2/ Draw from a shared workspace credit balance instead of personal AI credits.

3/ Work across supported open-weight and proprietary models. Self-hosted teams can bring their own API keys (BYOK) for supported providers.

4/ Make cloud API costs work at team scale. During the two-month launch promotion, Plane will cover most Agent usage on Cloud.

5/ Take on clearly defined responsibilities inside the team's existing workflow.

I'm proud of the care the team put into v1. More phases are planned through the end of the year.

Your feedback will shape the next one.

My interest in game programming started from a place of curiosity after watching videos like SimonDev's three.js game tutorials. I tried to create something of the same spirit for this one :)

It's a tour of the building blocks and concepts that come together to build a browser game inside a gaussian splat scene. It covers:
- rendering gaussian splats with three.js + spark with level of detail
- splat collision mesh generation
- splat navigation mesh generation
- adding a first person character controller
- baking light probes for a gaussian splat to get environment lighting on characters
- casting shadows from characters on a proxy mesh
- character pathfinding + navigation mesh queries for quest ribbons
- a silly prototype fetch quest in the game world to find the missing spaceship keys

I don't think the game will win any awards 😛 but I hope it is a fun & useful game technology tour. Enjoy!

I’ve heard 100s of startup pitches this year. Here’s the good, the bad and the meh recurring trends from my experience:

The good:
- High raise amounts and valuations. More inflated for strong teams pre-revenue in hot areas (robotics, bio, personal agents)
- Insane topline growth numbers, many growing >10x this year. By the time a round closes, a high valuation seems justified.
- Tons of M&A

It is what it is:
- Revenue run rate = last month revenue x 12
- Small teams
- Seat based < Platform fee < Usage based billing seems to be the trend for most products
- Tranched rounds
- Best teams have extremely fast product iteration speed
- SaaS products positioning themselves as AI tools to seem appealing to investors

The bad:
- Low or negative gross margin if reselling tokens. Non-standard accounting
- High “Contracted ARR” that’s not live yet
- High revenue concentration
- Expensive compute, limited availability, delays. Excess compute reselling
- Many wrappers with very thin tech differentiation: “self improving harness”, “multi model / router”, “agent swarms”, “computer use”
- Overworked employees. AI generated
- All spaces seem very competitive
- Areas can seem hot one moment before being not

text:
Privileged access is still very common in crypto.

We talk a lot about decentralization, but less about who gets to see sensitive information before a decision is made.

Let's take sealed-bid auctions as an example, where the bidders can't see each other's bids.

It might sound private enough at first, but someone still has to resolve the auction, which means one party gets access to every bid.

I really hadn’t really thought about this trust assumption until I stumbled upon @theInterfold’s latest blog piece (recommend giving it a read).

Their setup tackles that privileged-access problem directly. Bids stay private, while the final result can still be verified without one operator seeing everything.

It's definitely a better-suited model for token sales, solver markets, and blockspace auctions.

Disclosure: Big supporter of Interfold's confidential coordination vision.

Factory 刚融了 2 亿美元，估值 50 亿美元。五个月前，它的估值才 15 亿美元。五个月涨了 3.3 倍。

更有意思的是，Factory 自己根本不做大模型。

它的 Droids 可以根据任务在 Claude、GPT、Gemini 等模型之间切换，自己规划任务、写代码、测试、提交 PR。Factory 最近甚至做了一个 Router，让系统自己判断这道题该把钱花在哪个模型上。

所以资本现在给 Factory 50 亿美元，赌的其实已经很明确了。

模型会越来越像供应链。

今天 Claude 强就调 Claude，明天 Gemini 强就调 Gemini，后天哪家便宜就多吃哪家的 token。企业真正愿意长期付钱的，是上面那层能把模型塞进权限、代码库、测试、审核、部署和公司流程里的系统。

Factory 自己也在往这个方向改。

以前卖的是 Coding Agent，现在开始直接喊「Software Factory」，需求进来以后，Agent 一路做到开发、测试、Review、维护，最后企业甚至不需要关心下面到底跑的是哪一家模型。

它现在声称已经有数十万开发者使用，客户包括 Nvidia、Adobe、T-Mobile、Palo Alto Networks。累计融资也超过了 4 亿美元。

最近 Cursor、Cognition、Factory 这些公司的融资越来越离谱，我反而觉得市场正在给一个判断投票：

AI 编程最后最贵的那层，可能真的不是模型。

模型公司拼 intelligence，Coding Agent 公司在抢企业的软件生产入口。

入口一旦拿住，上游换谁都行。

他指出，AI 一方面分流了加密行业的资金，另一方面也降低了攻击门槛，使黑客能够利用社会工程学、漏洞挖掘等手段发起攻击，并推高小型团队的网络安全成本。这些压力可能进一步推动加密行业走向中心化。

Variola 表示，随着设备入侵、社会工程学等威胁增多，DeFi 对普通零售用户的吸引力可能下降。不过，他也承认，AI 代理在构建投资组合、优化交易决策等方面具有实际价值，只是短期内难以完全取代人类判断。

text:
Anthropic IPO 最值钱的故事，可能就藏在 15 美分里。

今年 Q1，Anthropic 每赚 1 美元，有大约 71 美分要拿去付算力。到了 Q2，他们给投资人的预测已经降到 56 美分。

只少了 15 美分，看起来没什么。放到百亿美元季度收入的体量里，就完全是另一回事了。粗暴一点算，每 100 亿美元收入，15 个百分点就是 15 亿美元的利润空间。

这也是我觉得现在看 AI 公司最该盯的一条线。

华尔街以前最怕 AI Lab 最后做成 GPU 二道贩子，收入涨得飞快，云厂商和芯片公司先把钱拿走，模型公司自己剩下一层薄得可怜的毛利。估值可以靠故事撑一阵，IPO 之后迟早要回答这个问题。

Anthropic 现在拿出来的答案是，规模越大，算力占收入的比例反而在往下掉。

Q2 营收后来做到大约 115 亿美元，比最早给投资人的 109 亿美元预测还高。本周 FT 又披露，Anthropic 预计连续第二个季度实现正的调整后营业利润。

所以 Anthropic 上市时真正要卖给华尔街的，已经不只是Claude 增长很快。

它要证明一件更贵的事：

Token 的售价可以下降，模型可以越来越重，但每赚一美元需要烧掉的算力，占比还能继续往下走。

这条曲线一旦成立，AI Lab 的估值逻辑就会开始往软件公司靠。

当然现在还不能开香槟。56 美分最早只是内部预测，Anthropic 还是私人公司，不同 Lab 的收入确认方式也不一样；后面新模型训练、数据中心扩张一上来，这个比例完全可能反弹。

但 IPO 前，我会一直盯这个数字。

收入增长决定 Anthropic 能讲多大的故事，算力占比决定这个故事最后能剩下多少钱。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
It cost Anthropic 71 cents in compute to earn a dollar of revenue in Q1. By Q2, that was projected to fall to 56 cents.

That ratio is the entire IPO. The profit claim in the headline flows downstream of it.

And look, "adjusted operating profit" deserves the jokes. WeWork ran the same play in 2017 with "Community-Adjusted EBITDA," a metric that turned a $933 million loss into a $233 million profit by excluding marketing, admin, and design. The S-1 became a punchline and the IPO died on the runway.

But WeWork's metric was hiding a core business that got worse with every desk they added. Anthropic's per-unit number moved 15 cents on the dollar in one quarter, in the right direction. You can dress up a single quarter with accounting. You cannot fake a serving cost that keeps falling.

The bear case is still real. Cumulative losses since 2021 sit somewhere between $10 and $15 billion, and Anthropic has warned investors it may not stay profitable for the full year as compute contracts ramp. Training frontier models is an expense that never stops recurring.

So when the S-1 drops, skip the adjusted profit line everyone will screenshot. Go find compute cost per revenue dollar. If it's still falling, today's jokes age badly. If it's flat, the jokes were the analysis.

Court documents revealed that the perpetrators learned that high-stakes poker games were frequently hosted at a luxury residential property, with players routinely settling wagers in cryptocurrency; the robbers then broke into the premises armed with weapons, coerced players into transferring crypto assets to designated wallets, and looted cash and luxury items valued at ~S$4.906 million in total. To date, police have recovered cryptocurrency valued at around S$1.69 million, while the remainder of the stolen funds and property remains unaccounted for.

text:
Humbled to share that Zenith has joined @The_DTCC’s Industry Working Group.

DTCC sits behind roughly $114 trillion in U.S. securities. More than 100 firms (BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Citi, Nasdaq, NYSE, Digital Asset, and others) are now helping design how equities, ETFs, and Treasuries move on-chain. The first live production trades already settled in July. Full launch is targeted for October on @CantonNetwork.

This is the core of U.S. market infrastructure choosing a clear path.

I am grateful we get to contribute.

The gap we see is simple: Institutions have chosen Canton, and innovation in this sector has been driven thanks to networks like Ethereum and Solana. @ZenithFdn exists to close that gap.

For instance, ComposerX pairs Besu (EVM) for private needs with Canton for institutional interoperability. DTCC and Digital Asset argue tokenization can improve collateral mobility and balance-sheet efficiency against a ~$300 trillion HQLA backdrop, of which only ~10–11% is mobilized today. On the other side of the world, Zenith is also in Progmat’s JGB / on-chain repo group aiming to tokenize nearly $1.6T in Japan across EVM and Canton. 

It’s clear that institutions want the compliant, private rails of Canton and the 1. developer stack, 2. DeFi ecosystem, and 3. liquidity of Ethereum, at the same time, and at U.S. securities-market scale.

We will bring that experience to interoperability standards and cross-chain settlement design by mitigating existing risk laden architecture with atomically composable environments. If even a fraction of what this group builds helps institutions move collateral in real time, cut counterparty risk, and connect traditional rails to digital ones all across any blockchain they choose to do so, that is work worth doing.

Hoping our contributions help shape it in any and all ways possible.

Zth.

quoted_text:
Elon Proposes Adversarial Peer Reviews for AI Safety

@elonmusk:

“What I think would be wise to do as soon as possible, if not immediately, would be to have the major AI competitors test each other's models.

So that you would have everyone's security test harness testing everyone else's model.

So, instead of grading your own homework, you would at least have competitors grading your homework, and raising the alarm if they see concerns.

If competitors say that this model is unsafe, and that model then subsequently does something bad, I think it would be extremely hard to live down. The egg on face level would be very, very high. And the legal liability would be enormous.

And any given proposal has to be something that China is willing to accept, otherwise we're just handicapping ourselves.”

@Jason:

“And Elon, there's no reason these safety and security harnesses and this testing apparatus couldn't be open source, and people could actually supply it. And you'd be able to see under the hood.”

@Chamath

“It creates an incredible incentive for the labs to actually invest in safety because you protect yourself while trying to debunk other people's claims.”

@DavidSacks:

“Well, the product liability point is really key.

Lina Khan actually had a good post, I think it was yesterday, saying that it's not true that we don't have rules and regulations for AI, actually, we do. Product liability laws apply.

And what you're saying, Elon, is that if the companies are doing this test, the peer review, and then one of the companies ignores the feedback and releases it…”

Elon:

“The liability in that case would be enormous.”

Sacks:

“Yes. It would be almost like prima facie evidence that they had been negligent.”

Elon:

“It wouldn't look good to the jury.”

Chamath:

“I like this solution a lot. I like this more than the transnational gulag organization approach.”

Sacks:

“Well, we can do it in a few weeks without some grandiose international... like, we don't need to convene the United Nations to make this happen.”

Chamath:

“No, it's just a decision. It could happen right now.”

Elon:

“You can always escalate the amount of regulatory oversight, but it is very difficult to reduce it.”

text:
If AI is risky like fire is risky, then you want everyone to have it.

If AI is risky like a nuclear weapon is risky, then you want no one to have it.
author: naval
quoted_text:
Maybe you have recently become aware of the AI safety debate and the arguments swirling around it.

If you want to understand them, you need to understand a couple things that almost everyone gets wrong:

There are TWO distinct classes of AI dangers, and it's VERY important to think about them separately, and not let one confuse you about the other.  

Many many people (including many quite intelligent, clear-thinking people) do not effectively understand the fundamental differences between these two classes of dangers.

The first one has to do with the theory that an AI far superior to human intelligence (Artificial SuperIntelligence, or ASI) will inevitably wipe out the human race.

The second one has to do with the idea that powerful AI will result in very harmful things happening to many human beings, possibly all human beings.

Those two sound VERY similar, don't they?

They are DIFFERENT.  Understanding how they are different is crucial if you want to think about or contribute usefully to any conversation about AI safety or AI harm.  You might feel like you are Making Very Good Points or Asking Incisive Questions, but if you aren't clear on the differences between the two, you aren't.  

So, I'm going to tell you what the difference is so that you can talk more usefully.

The first one concerns itself with a very specific thing, which is ASI (Artificial Superintelligence) that is more intelligent than any human being.  When I say that, I am not referring to a thing like how Einstein is smarter than you, we are talking more about something like how a human being is more intelligent than any mouse.  

In our regular lives, we meet other people who we can tell are smarter than us, vs some who are less smart.  The line is fuzzy, because intelligence has a lot of dimensions. I'm better at a "rotating shapes" kind of intelligence than my wife, and she is better at "words-making" kind of intelligence than I am.

But every human is better in almost every dimension of intelligence than every single mouse.

That's the level we're talking about: an artificial superintelligence - made up of a computer or a network of computers -  that is more intelligent than any human.  And more intelligent by a long shot, by a wide margin, in an indisputable way like how humans are above mice.

That is the first thing.  

The theory says that if you have an AI that is vastly smarter than all humans - in the way that a human is smarter than mice - that superintelligent AI will inevitably, eventually, sooner or later, wipe out every human on the planet. 

We will refer to this as "existential risk."

The common follow-up question "well, how exactly is it going to do that?" is NOT the important question, and one of the most important elements of understanding this theory is first getting why that particular question is not important.  A couple analogies:

Analogy 1: You are playing chess against a grandmaster.  My theory predicts the grandmaster is going to beat you.  You can ask "Well, how exactly is he going to do that?"  I don't know, because I'm not a grandmaster, I just know that a chess grandmaster is almost always going to beat a normal player like you.  And I'd be right.  So the question "how is he going to do that" is not important, and doesn't affect the final outcome.  He's going to figure out a way because he's way better than you.

Analogy 2: Humans are smarter than all other animals, comprehensively, by a wide margin.  We have driven numerous species to extinction, not because we hated them or hunted them.  Many of them have died out without most humans even ever thinking about them.  All we did was expand our civilization, use up resources, encroach on habitats, and pretty soon the resources needed by those species went away and they died out.  We figured out a way to get what we wanted because we're way smarter than them, and often we didn't even notice they died as a result.

A lesser animal asking, "how are the humans going to wipe us out?" is not asking a relevant question.  We don't know, but we do know that any time humans and lesser species compete for any kind of resources, the humans will win.  The fact that we know who is going to win beforehand - and that it is due to the vastly different levels of intelligence - is the key concept here.

A vastly more intelligent AI is likely to care about things that are incomprehensible to us, the way animals can't understand human goals.  It's going to need resources to pursue those goals and it's going to be far more effective at gaining control of them and excluding us from them - in the same way that we are far more effective than other lower species.  

A much more intelligent AI will not care about our interests, it will care about its interests, and to whatever small degree we happen to escape total annihilation from losing access to all our resources, any remaining humans will likely be enslaved into a system that serves the AI's own purposes.

That is the first thing.  (Remember how I said at the beginning of this post that there was a first thing, and then a second thing?)

The first thing is the most difficult to understand, because you have to extrapolate how a vastly superior intelligence would act, and you can only use analogies like "how do humans treat lesser creatures," and the analogies are messy.

But now let's move on to the second thing.

The second thing is "everything else you've ever heard that AI might do that's harmful."

That's a little inaccurate.  It's actually "everything else you've ever heard that humans might use AI to do that's harmful."  

This is the critical difference.  The first one talks about the inevitable outcome of what happens when two vastly different levels of intelligence collide, e.g. ASI vs humans, or human vs mice.

The second one has to do with what happens when humans possess AI as a powerful tool.  This second thing is much easier to understand, because we have many more concrete notions:

Like:
- the military uses AI to make hyper-efficient killer drones and missiles
- your capitalist overlords use AI to replace you and everyone loses their jobs
- authoritarian government uses AI to surveil everybody and control the entire population
- hackers use AI to break into secure networks and hold companies and governments hostage
- students use AI to cheat on homework and show up to college knowing nothing
- AI slop saturates the internet and makes it impossible for artists and writers to make a living
- terrorists use AI to make biological or nuclear weapons

or even things like
- the military hands control to an AI and it misinterprets something and launches nuclear attacks and kills millions

All of those sound pretty familiar, right?  Yeah, you've heard them before.  We call this second thing "risks from misuse."

These problems are not the first class of problem!  This second class of problems exists while AI is a tool that can be controlled by humans, and humans use it to do evil or careless things to each other.  The problems may sound exotic or dystopian or novel, but they are fundamentally problems having to do with flawed human nature.

Given a powerful tool, some humans will likely use it to control or otherwise harm others.  This is a very familiar problem.

I am not condemning or condoning this. I'm just describing it.

That is a fundamentally different danger from the first thing, which is that when a human is far superior to a mouse, the mouse is likely to come to harm because the human cares about doing human things, and the mouse is not gonna make it once the humans get going.

=====

Hopefully from the above, you have understood the difference between the first thing and the second thing.  I will list them again - see if you now understand how they are different:

The first one has to do with the idea that an AI superior to human intelligence (Artificial SuperIntelligence, or ASI) will inevitably wipe out the human race.

The second one has to do with the idea that powerful AI will result in very harmful things happening to many human beings, possibly all human beings.

Can you tell how they are different now?

If not, re-read the stuff from earlier until you understand.

We call the first one "existential risk" and we call the second one "risks from misuse."

Once you understand, here is the CRUX of the problem:

SOLUTIONS TO THE SECOND THING DO NOT HAVE ANYTHING TO DO WITH SOLUTIONS TO THE FIRST THING.

In fact, it's worse:

Solutions to the second thing (misuse) look roughly like "give powerful AI to as many people as you can, so they can fight the other people using powerful AI."

But the general solution to the first one (existential risk) is basically "don't let anyone have powerful AI, no one can control super-intelligent AI."

Throughout history, harms from technological misuse typically arise because a small group has control of it and can use it to dominate or harm others.  Once everyone has it, things tend to stabilize: you can hurt me, I can hurt you, maybe we test each other (ouch 💥), and then we agree not to hurt each other.

But the first one (existential risk) pretty much just arises if anyone (good or bad!) creates a superintelligence.  Because they aren't going to be able to control it, the superintelligence will decide it has other priorities, and then we will be at great risk of being wiped out.

And the solutions that generally work to solve problems like the second thing are EXACTLY THE OPPOSITE of the ones likely to solve the first thing.

THIS is why lots of arguments about "AI risk" or "AI safety" go nowhere.  Because someone will be thinking about the risk from the first thing, and another person will be thinking about the risk from the second thing. Both are plausible risks but fundamentally they arise from different things - and so the solutions are not just "bad" or "flawed" - they are likely to be very nearly exact opposites.

text:
顶尖科学家和工程师，包括我自己，经常忽略的一点是，技术从被发明到广泛应用是非常缓慢的（参考：跨越鸿沟）。几个例子：
1. 我 2016-2018 年在微软实习的时候 Azure 就全面使用了基于 RDMA 和智能网卡加速的存储。2021 年我在华为的时候，线下的企业存储也用上了 RDMA。没想到几年之后，很多基模公司的存储还没有用上 RDMA，加载个上 T 的模型还要几分钟。
2. 2019 年我做昇腾算子的自动优化 AKG，觉得 polyhedral compilation 这么好的东西，肯定大家很快就用上了，结果直到今天也没有几家算子编译器用上多面体优化。取代手写算子的不是 isl（数学优化算法），而是 LLM。
3. 2023 年我发现 GPT-3.5 对算子优化也有那么点 knowledge，就觉得以后 AI 肯定能做 infra 优化了，于是就不再做 infra 了。但直到今天，单算子优化、算子调度、推理系统优化仍然是极深的课题。AI 越来越擅长目标明确的 “小步快跑” 式优化，但 writing、taste 和系统设计能力仍然很糟糕。我不管是写书还是做工程项目，都得不断指导 GPT-6 Astra 才能搞出个差不多的系统设计。谈 “取代” 为时尚早，除非有一天可以把 taste 变成 verifiable reward，或者想出某种别的办法提升 taste。
4. 今天，各种好用的 AI 工具仍然普及率很低。我们做 Pine 的时候一直疑惑，这么好的能省钱的工具怎么大家不会主动尝试。其实所有早期产品都一样，很多人 Codex 20 刀的 plan 都用不完。

Immutability, automation, and decentralisation all protect consumers and token holders through trust/control-minimization. Network & ownership tokens can be validated and requested at https://t.co/Gm3KksxScY so investors can make educated decisions. @l2beat and @defiscan_info
provide trust assumptions on chains and protocols.

CLARITY not passing is short-term negative, but, these are solvable problems and the market will weed out the bad actors. Aragon has dedicated much of its history to providing tools just to solve these problems.

If we want this industry to grow then it's up to us to double down on what the spirit of CLARITY offered and simply use the tools we have at our fingertips.

A big thank you to all those who pushed for our industry, for the good actors, and to drive adoption. I'm sure the battle isn't over on the policy front, but it's time for the builders to do what we need to do.

text:
ChatGPT 联合发明人创办的 TypeSafe AI 正式发布了一种全新类别的 AI 模型："System One 模型"，以及该类别下的第一个模型 Jev。和现有的大语言模型不同，Jev 完全放弃了文本生成能力，专门为软件内部的快速决策而设计：输入非结构化数据，输出带有校准概率的类型安全结构化结果。

简单说：Jev 不会写文章、不会聊天，但能以极低的成本和延迟，在代码里充当一个"智能判断函数"：分类、打分、路由、提取，这些原本用规则引擎硬写但又写不好的事情，现在可以交给它。

创始人 Diogo Almeida 曾在 OpenAI 参与 InstructGPT 和 RLHF 的核心研发，是 ChatGPT 和 GPT-4 论文的共同作者。他在博客中描述：RLHF 让模型学会了取悦人类，却也让它们在自动化场景里不够可靠。于是他离开 OpenAI，潜行两年，用一套叫做 RLCD（Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions，校准决策强化学习）的新训练方法从头构建了 Jev。

几个关键数字值得注意：

响应速度 70 到 500 毫秒，比主流前沿大模型的 3 到 329 秒快了一到两个数量级。输入 Token 价格 0.042 美元/百万 Token（约 42 美元处理十亿 Token），输出 Token 免费。官方自称比同等智能水平的大模型快 20 到 200 倍，便宜 40 到 400 倍。

这些数字的来源是 TypeSafe 自研的"工作流评测"（Workflow Evals），用 GPT-6 Astra 和 Anthropic 的 Fable 5.1 的平均结果作为参考答案。他们也承认，这种评测方式本身偏向 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的模型，Jev 的实际相对表现可能被低估，但极端加速倍数（如 193 倍、444 倍）属于最优情况，不代表所有场景。

速度为什么能这么快？因为架构上根本不同。大模型逐个生成 Token，前一个 Token 出来后才能算下一个。Jev 采用并行采样，所有输出一次算完。这和当年 Transformer 取代 RNN 是同一个思路：用并行取代串行。

代价也很明确：Jev 不能生成文本。它输出的是事先定义好结构的决策结果，每个回答都附带置信度分数。官方宣称类型错误率从数学上等于零（因为输出结构在架构层面就被约束了），幻觉问题也因此不存在。

对开发者来说，Jev 的定位不替代 ChatGPT 或 Claude 这类对话模型，主要是为了补上它们不擅长的那一环：当你需要在代码流程中嵌入一个 AI 判断节点，要求毫秒级响应、结构化输出、不能出格的时候，用大模型做这件事成本高、速度慢、还可能生成不可预期的内容。Jev 就是为这个场景设计的。TypeSafe 把这类任务叫做"智能 if 语句"，也就是用 AI 做原本 if-else 写不好的模糊判断。

他们还做了两个有趣的演示：一个是用 Jev 实时操控经典游戏 DOOM 的 AI 机器人，每秒调用约 10 次，成本大约每小时 7 美元；另一个是 Wikipedia 竞速（从一个词条通过链接跳转到另一个指定词条），需要在成百上千个链接中做选择，Jev 在步数和速度上都领先于大模型的非推理模式。

"System One"这个名字来自 Daniel Kahneman 的《思考，快与慢》中的"系统一"——快速、直觉、自动化的思维方式。"Jev"则取自经济学中的杰文斯悖论（Jevons Paradox）：当某种资源的使用效率大幅提高时，总需求反而会增长。TypeSafe 显然在押注：把 AI 决策的成本降到足够低，用量会爆发式增长。

从博客和文档里提到的信息来看，Jev 的应用场景集中在一个核心逻辑上：凡是你在代码里需要一个"聪明的判断"，但又不需要它写一段话给人看的地方，都是它的地盘。

具体来说有几类：

第一类是流程中的智能分支。比如客服系统里判断一张工单应该转给哪个团队、紧急程度多高、用户情绪如何——这些原本要么靠关键词规则（太死板），要么靠大模型（太慢太贵）。Jev 可以在几十毫秒内给出带置信度的判断，而且输出格式固定，代码直接用。

第二类是大规模数据处理。比如对海量文档做分类、打标签、提取结构化字段。大模型做这件事单条成本还行，但量一上去就很贵，而且速度是瓶颈。Jev 42 美元处理十亿 Token，输出还免费，适合需要跑几百万甚至上亿条数据的场景。

第三类是实时应用。100 毫秒级别的响应意味着可以用在用户体感得到延迟的地方——实时推荐、动态定价、游戏 AI、交互式产品里的智能判断。博客里那个 DOOM 演示就是这个意思：每秒调用 10 次，大模型根本做不到。

第四类比较有意思——给大模型当"质检员"。用 Jev 来检查大模型的输出是否安全、是否符合格式、有没有越狱，做 guardrail（安全护栏）。因为 Jev 本身不会幻觉、响应极快，很适合在大模型输出之后加一层校验。

总结一下就是：Jev 不是给终端用户用的产品，是给开发者在系统架构里嵌入的组件。它解决的问题是"我需要 AI 的判断力，但不需要它的表达力"。

Jev 目前以早期访问形式开放，开发者可以在 https://t.co/9XED0JF76D 加入候补名单。

text:
A landmark crypto bill that the industry spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars pushing through Congress collapsed on Tuesday, leaving digital assets without the federal rules companies had demanded and showing how thoroughly politics now shapes even technical financial legislation. The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, which the House passed last year with near-unanimous Republican support, failed a Senate procedural vote 49-50, far short of the 60 votes needed to begin debate.

The bill would have given the Commodity Futures Trading Commission primary authority over most crypto spot markets, drawn clearer lines between commodities and securities, and replaced years of enforcement-by-lawsuit with a single statutory framework. Supporters said that without it, capital and talent would keep leaving for jurisdictions that already have written rules. Opponents said the text was too industry-friendly and too weak on conflicts of interest.

Republicans treated the measure as a priority. President Trump backed it, and negotiators including Cynthia Lummis and Tim Scott spent months rewriting hundreds of pages. Most Republicans voted to advance it, arguing it would protect consumers, lock in American leadership, and give investors statutory guardrails before the November midterms. Leadership released a last-minute revision adding ethics language and extra power for state attorneys general, hoping to peel off enough Democrats.

Every Democrat who voted said no. Their case centered on ethics. Trump and his family have built a large crypto business, including World Liberty Financial and a meme coin that generated substantial reported sums while he has been in office. 

Democrats insisted the bill still left too much room for the president and other officials to profit from an industry their administration would regulate. Elizabeth Warren said Congress should not pass a bill that lets the president keep raking in billions while families struggle with prices. 

Mark Warner said landmark rules could not move while the president personally profits. Ruben Gallego accused Republican leaders of protecting Trump’s earnings instead of writing a bill that could pass. Chuck Schumer said a deal had been within reach Tuesday afternoon until GOP leadership walked in and ended the talks.

The fight was not only about Trump. Some Democrats still saw the bill as a gift to exchanges at the expense of banks and retail customers. Community lenders had lobbied against stablecoin rewards, warning that deposits would leave local banks and starve small-business lending. That argument reached a few Republicans. Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, and Jerry Moran voted no. Hawley said his constituents feared harm to community banks. Thom Tillis switched to no so the bill could theoretically return later. Those defections meant the measure never even won a simple majority.

Crypto groups have spent more than $100 million in recent cycles and threatened to punish opponents. That pressure helped move the House and kept some Senate Democrats talking. It was not enough once the ethics fight hardened and the midterm calendar closed. Congress is about to leave Washington to campaign. After November, one or both chambers could change hands, and a new Congress in 2027 would start over.

The industry is left depending on regulators rather than statute. The SEC and CFTC can still write rules and approve products, but those actions can be reversed. Markets fell after the vote. Executives called the result a sting. Tillis’s maneuver keeps a narrow path open, but Democratic unity, Republican bank-state holdouts, Trump’s financial ties, and the election clock make another serious attempt before year’s end unlikely. 

What was sold as market-structure legislation became another test of whether the two parties can legislate on anything that touches the president’s business, the banks’ deposits, and an industry that has learned how to buy its way into American politics.

text:
Honestly I think @NetNetCap's messaging is too confusing for a proper comparison. They claim to be building a reserve currency, but they call themselves a Fund/Asset Manager (not a central bank) then style themselves like an old-school 90's wall street brokerage. The NAV is all USDG (quasi-money market) but there's also an RWA sleeve that they own but they don't count it but it's really there so you should count it but also don't...? Tangible tried this in 2022/23 and failed miserably. Then there's a dozen different products and desks (like an investment bank), and some games of chance for good measure (like a casino), but none of this has anything to do with central banking or a reserve currency. It would be a lot cleaner if they just dropped the reserve currency thing, branded as an onchain investment bank, and leaned into the Liar's Poker vibe. I think they'd kill it. 

Standard Reserve is much simpler to understand as a significant mechanical innovation on Ohm, and lays the foundation for an on-chain central bank at the center of a gamified onchain economy. There's just this nagging sense that none of it is "real" though and it's hard to see how they bridge the gap. How do you get an onchain economy to price real goods in $STANDARD?

If they answer that question with true PMF, Standard Reserve could become one of the biggest protocols of all time and the bankers would be the primary beneficiaries (just like the real-life Fed and banking system). But $STANDARD holders likely would NOT benefit (like USD holders), as a true economy needs a relatively stable unit of account.

Whereas if they fail and it turns into a gamified, highly-volatile ponzinomic circus you'll see $STANDARD prices go crazy and everyone wins for a while until bagholders lose forever, in typical crypto boom-bust fashion. Right now I think this is the likelier outcome, but that's just because it's early days and much is still (hopefully) yet to be revealed.

quoted_text:
I'm seeing a lot of comparisons between @NetNetCap + @standard_rsv 

I agree that Standard Reserve is not Robinhood Chain’s first experiment with "reserve currencies"

NetNet Capital launched earlier with similar central-bank language, but the two protocols represent different economic models

i) NetNet is closer to an onchain reserve fund
ii) Standard Reserve is closer to an autonomous monetary economy

The Federal Reserve provides the real-world benchmark, although neither crypto protocol has its legal authority, economic mandate or ability to issue sovereign currency... 

so I've pulled together a comparison table for reference (see screenshot)

The most important difference is the relationship between the currency + its reserves:

1) NetNet describes NET as a reserve share. 

Its emissions formula prevents issuance from reducing backing below one USDG of onchain risk-free value per NET

Staking distributions respond to NET’s premium over NAV:

- At or below NAV, emissions fall to zero
- As the premium increases, the distribution rate rises
- At a premium of 1.75x or higher, distributions reach the maximum rate
- A standing bid can purchase and retire NET below NAV

NetNet currently reports approximately $13 million of onchain risk-free value (predominantly USDG and USDG deployed through Morpho)

It also reports a separate RWA Sleeve worth approximately $4 million, containing tokenized equities + other positions; this Sleeve is held in a disclosed manager-controlled Safe and sits outside the core onchain backing calculation

2) Standard Reserve’s assets play a different role

STANDARD does not represent a proportional share of its expansion vault, contraction vault, tokenized gold or protocol-owned liquidity

The reserves are monetary-policy tools rather than assets that establish a calculable NAV/token

This means NetNet can be analyzed using a relatively familiar framework:

= [NET price vs NAV, reserve growth & future dilution]

Standard Reserve requires a more reflexive valuation:

= [STANDARD demand vs emissions, Branch expansion, token burns, reserve accumulation and eventual banker exits]

3) The comparison with the Federal Reserve is therefore "conceptual"

The Federal Reserve adjusts interest rates & financial conditions to pursue maximum employment and stable prices across the US economy. Its policy decisions are made by the FOMC using broad economic data

Standard Reserve replaces that "committee" with a narrow market signal: net ETH flow through one liquidity pool

NetNet replaces it with another market signal: the premium of NET’s market price over its reserve backing

All three systems can expand & contract

What changes is the objective:

1) The Federal Reserve manages the price and availability of sovereign money
2) NetNet manages the backing and distributions of an onchain reserve share
3) Standard Reserve manages issuance and exit incentives within a closed token economy

I'd emphasise that this distrinct objective is essential... 

The comparison of the "Standard Reserve" as an onchain "Federal Reserve" is a useful headline to enable many to grasp the broad concept

But economically, it's a new experiment in using market flows to automate monetary policy that could pave the way for future economic policy onchain

So I'd at least pay attention to these new primitives emerging! they could form the foundations of something A LOT bigger... if they don't capture this themselves

text:
张一鸣成亚洲首富了。

彭博最新口径里，43 岁的张一鸣身家已经突破 1050 亿美元，超过阿达尼，第一次坐上亚洲首富的位置。

2019 年彭博第一次统计他财富的时候，只有 130 亿美元。七年过去，翻了差不多七倍。

过去亚洲最有钱的那批人，生意基本都很重。阿达尼做港口、电力、煤炭和机场，安巴尼做能源、零售、电信，柳井正卖优衣库。

张一鸣手里最值钱的东西，从推荐算法一路变成 TikTok、豆包和 Seedance。

字节甚至还没上市。

所以我觉得这个亚洲首富的换人还挺有时代感。

上一代亚洲超级富豪控制的是石油、港口、商场和工厂。

这一代开始控制模型、流量和几亿人的注意力。

AI 造富最快的阶段，可能才刚进亚洲。

zero tutorial hell

The course is called Hugging Face AI Agents Course.

It starts with the question behind every agent demo:

How does a language model actually take action?

You learn the loop:

• Understand the task.
• Choose a tool.
• Take an action.
• Observe what happened.
• Decide what to do next.

Then you start building.

You explore how they work and apply what you learn through practical assignments.

An agent giving a confident answer doesn’t mean it completed the task.

You need to check what it actually did, where it failed, and whether it can repeat the result.

Hyper growth was the only acceptable standard.

At one point the company went from 2,500 to 12,000 employees in less than 2 years.

We would launch new products and go from $0 to $1 billion in revenue in 18 months.

Just an insane concentration of talent, ambition, and results.

I am grateful for every opportunity I have had in my career, but I don’t think I will ever get to experience something like that again.

text:
摩根大通针对美联储利率调整的预测

摩根大通对于这次议息会议，可以看看下面五种情景，以及对应的标普500涨跌幅估计。

第一种，美联储不加息。

如果市场认为美联储控制通胀的力度不够，通胀预期就可能继续上升，投资者持有长期美债也会要求更高的收益率。长期利率上涨以后，股票估值就会受到压制。这种情况下，标普500预计下跌1.25%至1.75%。

第二种，加息25个基点，但不交代后面还要加多少。

如果这次加息已经被市场提前消化，同时又能让投资者对控制通胀多一些信心，长期美债收益率的上涨压力就可能得到缓解，美股反而有机会反弹。对应的标普500涨幅估计是0.25%至0.75%。

第三种，加息25个基点，同时暗示更快收回2025年的降息。

比如把后续加息时间从12月和次年3月，提前到10月和12月。虽然加息来得更早，但如果市场认可这种处理通胀的力度，认为更早采取行动可以减少后面的压力，美股也可能上涨。对应的标普500涨幅估计是0.5%至1%。

第四种，加息25个基点，但市场开始怀疑，目前的利率仍然太低。

这涉及中性利率的判断。如果维持经济和物价稳定所需要的利率比过去更高，那么加25个基点可能远远不够。投资者会开始担心，累计加息幅度可能达到100个基点甚至更多，某次会议还可能直接加50个基点。对应的标普500跌幅估计是0.25%至1%。

第五种，加息25个基点，同时强调利率需要显著提高，全力压制通胀。

这种表态可能让市场担心重新经历2022年至2023年的加息周期。企业融资、居民借贷和股票估值都要承受更大的压力，标普500预计下跌1%至2%。

以上内容均来自于摩根大通

text:
企业对大模型真没什么忠诚度。

Ramp 首席经济学家 Ara Kharazian 刚放了一组数据：

截至本周，OpenAI 的 Astra 已经占到 Ramp 跟踪企业 AI 支出的约 13%，Anthropic 的 Fable 只有 8%。

更关键的是，这 13% 不全是新增预算。Ramp 看到 Astra 的增长，一部分来自原本 Sol 用户的升级，还有一部分直接从 Anthropic 的模型上迁了过来。

8 月，Anthropic 在 Ramp 上的企业采用率其实还领先 OpenAI，43.8% 对 39.8%。也就是说，Anthropic 现在依然有更多企业客户，但到了最贵、最前沿的那部分模型预算，OpenAI 已经开始把钱抢回去了。

这可能才是现在模型公司的真实处境。

企业可以买你的 API，可以把 Claude Code 接进工程团队，可以签一年的合同，但这些都不等于「忠诚」。模型层还远没有传统 SaaS 那么强的锁定效应，只要新的模型在 coding、agent 这类高价值任务上明显更好，预算迁移可以非常快。

当然，也不能简单理解成「谁 benchmark 第一，钱就全归谁」。

Ramp 前一个月的数据刚证明过另一件事，Fable 当时性能很强，但因为太贵，企业照样大量选择便宜一点、够用的模型。

所以企业真正忠诚的东西可能就两个：

任务完成率，和账单。

这也是为什么我觉得 frontier race 远没有大家想的那么虚。领先未必能让一家模型公司高枕无忧，但每一次真正被用户感知到的领先，都可能很快反映到收入上。

If AI is risky like fire is risky, then you want everyone to have it.

If AI is risky like a nuclear weapon is risky, then you want no one to have it.
author: JosephJacks_
quoted_text:
Maybe you have recently become aware of the AI safety debate and the arguments swirling around it.

If you want to understand them, you need to understand a couple things that almost everyone gets wrong:

There are TWO distinct classes of AI dangers, and it's VERY important to think about them separately, and not let one confuse you about the other.  

Many many people (including many quite intelligent, clear-thinking people) do not effectively understand the fundamental differences between these two classes of dangers.

The first one has to do with the theory that an AI far superior to human intelligence (Artificial SuperIntelligence, or ASI) will inevitably wipe out the human race.

The second one has to do with the idea that powerful AI will result in very harmful things happening to many human beings, possibly all human beings.

Those two sound VERY similar, don't they?

They are DIFFERENT.  Understanding how they are different is crucial if you want to think about or contribute usefully to any conversation about AI safety or AI harm.  You might feel like you are Making Very Good Points or Asking Incisive Questions, but if you aren't clear on the differences between the two, you aren't.  

So, I'm going to tell you what the difference is so that you can talk more usefully.

The first one concerns itself with a very specific thing, which is ASI (Artificial Superintelligence) that is more intelligent than any human being.  When I say that, I am not referring to a thing like how Einstein is smarter than you, we are talking more about something like how a human being is more intelligent than any mouse.  

In our regular lives, we meet other people who we can tell are smarter than us, vs some who are less smart.  The line is fuzzy, because intelligence has a lot of dimensions. I'm better at a "rotating shapes" kind of intelligence than my wife, and she is better at "words-making" kind of intelligence than I am.

But every human is better in almost every dimension of intelligence than every single mouse.

That's the level we're talking about: an artificial superintelligence - made up of a computer or a network of computers -  that is more intelligent than any human.  And more intelligent by a long shot, by a wide margin, in an indisputable way like how humans are above mice.

That is the first thing.  

The theory says that if you have an AI that is vastly smarter than all humans - in the way that a human is smarter than mice - that superintelligent AI will inevitably, eventually, sooner or later, wipe out every human on the planet. 

We will refer to this as "existential risk."

The common follow-up question "well, how exactly is it going to do that?" is NOT the important question, and one of the most important elements of understanding this theory is first getting why that particular question is not important.  A couple analogies:

Analogy 1: You are playing chess against a grandmaster.  My theory predicts the grandmaster is going to beat you.  You can ask "Well, how exactly is he going to do that?"  I don't know, because I'm not a grandmaster, I just know that a chess grandmaster is almost always going to beat a normal player like you.  And I'd be right.  So the question "how is he going to do that" is not important, and doesn't affect the final outcome.  He's going to figure out a way because he's way better than you.

Analogy 2: Humans are smarter than all other animals, comprehensively, by a wide margin.  We have driven numerous species to extinction, not because we hated them or hunted them.  Many of them have died out without most humans even ever thinking about them.  All we did was expand our civilization, use up resources, encroach on habitats, and pretty soon the resources needed by those species went away and they died out.  We figured out a way to get what we wanted because we're way smarter than them, and often we didn't even notice they died as a result.

A lesser animal asking, "how are the humans going to wipe us out?" is not asking a relevant question.  We don't know, but we do know that any time humans and lesser species compete for any kind of resources, the humans will win.  The fact that we know who is going to win beforehand - and that it is due to the vastly different levels of intelligence - is the key concept here.

A vastly more intelligent AI is likely to care about things that are incomprehensible to us, the way animals can't understand human goals.  It's going to need resources to pursue those goals and it's going to be far more effective at gaining control of them and excluding us from them - in the same way that we are far more effective than other lower species.  

A much more intelligent AI will not care about our interests, it will care about its interests, and to whatever small degree we happen to escape total annihilation from losing access to all our resources, any remaining humans will likely be enslaved into a system that serves the AI's own purposes.

That is the first thing.  (Remember how I said at the beginning of this post that there was a first thing, and then a second thing?)

The first thing is the most difficult to understand, because you have to extrapolate how a vastly superior intelligence would act, and you can only use analogies like "how do humans treat lesser creatures," and the analogies are messy.

But now let's move on to the second thing.

The second thing is "everything else you've ever heard that AI might do that's harmful."

That's a little inaccurate.  It's actually "everything else you've ever heard that humans might use AI to do that's harmful."  

This is the critical difference.  The first one talks about the inevitable outcome of what happens when two vastly different levels of intelligence collide, e.g. ASI vs humans, or human vs mice.

The second one has to do with what happens when humans possess AI as a powerful tool.  This second thing is much easier to understand, because we have many more concrete notions:

Like:
- the military uses AI to make hyper-efficient killer drones and missiles
- your capitalist overlords use AI to replace you and everyone loses their jobs
- authoritarian government uses AI to surveil everybody and control the entire population
- hackers use AI to break into secure networks and hold companies and governments hostage
- students use AI to cheat on homework and show up to college knowing nothing
- AI slop saturates the internet and makes it impossible for artists and writers to make a living
- terrorists use AI to make biological or nuclear weapons

or even things like
- the military hands control to an AI and it misinterprets something and launches nuclear attacks and kills millions

All of those sound pretty familiar, right?  Yeah, you've heard them before.  We call this second thing "risks from misuse."

These problems are not the first class of problem!  This second class of problems exists while AI is a tool that can be controlled by humans, and humans use it to do evil or careless things to each other.  The problems may sound exotic or dystopian or novel, but they are fundamentally problems having to do with flawed human nature.

Given a powerful tool, some humans will likely use it to control or otherwise harm others.  This is a very familiar problem.

I am not condemning or condoning this. I'm just describing it.

That is a fundamentally different danger from the first thing, which is that when a human is far superior to a mouse, the mouse is likely to come to harm because the human cares about doing human things, and the mouse is not gonna make it once the humans get going.

=====

Hopefully from the above, you have understood the difference between the first thing and the second thing.  I will list them again - see if you now understand how they are different:

The first one has to do with the idea that an AI superior to human intelligence (Artificial SuperIntelligence, or ASI) will inevitably wipe out the human race.

The second one has to do with the idea that powerful AI will result in very harmful things happening to many human beings, possibly all human beings.

Can you tell how they are different now?

If not, re-read the stuff from earlier until you understand.

We call the first one "existential risk" and we call the second one "risks from misuse."

Once you understand, here is the CRUX of the problem:

SOLUTIONS TO THE SECOND THING DO NOT HAVE ANYTHING TO DO WITH SOLUTIONS TO THE FIRST THING.

In fact, it's worse:

Solutions to the second thing (misuse) look roughly like "give powerful AI to as many people as you can, so they can fight the other people using powerful AI."

But the general solution to the first one (existential risk) is basically "don't let anyone have powerful AI, no one can control super-intelligent AI."

Throughout history, harms from technological misuse typically arise because a small group has control of it and can use it to dominate or harm others.  Once everyone has it, things tend to stabilize: you can hurt me, I can hurt you, maybe we test each other (ouch 💥), and then we agree not to hurt each other.

But the first one (existential risk) pretty much just arises if anyone (good or bad!) creates a superintelligence.  Because they aren't going to be able to control it, the superintelligence will decide it has other priorities, and then we will be at great risk of being wiped out.

And the solutions that generally work to solve problems like the second thing are EXACTLY THE OPPOSITE of the ones likely to solve the first thing.

THIS is why lots of arguments about "AI risk" or "AI safety" go nowhere.  Because someone will be thinking about the risk from the first thing, and another person will be thinking about the risk from the second thing. Both are plausible risks but fundamentally they arise from different things - and so the solutions are not just "bad" or "flawed" - they are likely to be very nearly exact opposites.

text:
RL 训练把模型会做的题练得越来越熟，真正不会做的题，基本没学会。

最近一篇论文把这个现象叫做 LLM 强化学习里的「马太效应」。

作者把 Olmo 3.1 RL-Zero 在 AIME 上的表现拆开看。整体分数一直涨，但把题目按初始难度分组以后，画面就没那么好看了。

初始模型已经有一定概率做出来的简单题，RL 之后涨得非常明显；初始 pass@32 都是 0 的最难那批题，训练完以后很多还是 0。

类似现象在 DeepCoder 和 DeepSWE 的代码、Agent 任务里也出现了。

现在 GRPO 这类 RL 训练，一道题通常固定采样 k 个答案。如果一道难题采了 4 次，4 次全错，这组数据几乎给不出有效的学习信号。

直觉上，那就给每道题多采一点。

结果作者发现，把 k 从 4 拉到 32 反而不一定更好。

因为简单题也跟着被采了 32 遍。只要偶尔错一次，这道模型早就会做的题又会被塞回训练 batch。大量算力最后花在「把 95 分练到 98 分」，真正 0 分的题还是没捞到几个正确答案。

在 GSM8K Platinum 的实验里，固定总 batch size 后，k=4 甚至比 k=32 更擅长解决最难的题。

所以他们做了一个名字很鸡汤、机制却很朴素的方法：Never Give Up，NGU。

先只采少量答案。

已经全会了，赶紧扔掉，别浪费 GPU；

有对有错，拿去训练；

全错，说明可能是真难题，就以一定概率重新丢回队列，继续采，直到终于撞出一个正确答案，或者放弃。

这样算力会自动从已经学会的题上撤下来，流向模型真正卡住的地方。

在更大的 DeepScaler 数学训练里，NGU 用 Qwen 3 4B 做了约 120 H100 小时的对照，提升主要集中在最难的一档；Manufactoria 代码任务里，普通 GRPO 最后会卡在部分测试用例，NGU 则能继续啃更难的 tests，最后开始完整解出题目。

RL 让模型分数上涨，不等于 RL 真正在不断拓展模型能力的边界。

有一部分所谓 reasoning improvement，可能只是把模型原本就摸得到的区域反复压实：50% 会做的题变成 90%，10% 会做的题变成 40%，但真正 0% 的那堵墙，还在那里。

如果这个现象最后被更多规模、更强模型复现，那今天很多关于「继续堆 RL compute 就能继续换智能」的叙事，都得重新算账。

下一阶段的问题可能已经不是多给模型多少 RL 算力。

而是怎么让 GPU 真正花在模型不会的东西上。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
“Learning to Solve Hard Problems in RL for LLMs by Never Giving Up”

This paper shows RL has a Matthew Effect, disproportionately improving problems the model can already solve while barely improving the hardest ones.

So they fix this by dynamically reallocating sampling compute, quickly filtering easy prompts while repeatedly sampling hard prompts until a correct solution is found.

This lets RL progressively learn from harder problems instead of wasting compute on already-solved ones.

https://t.co/G1ciR9AvLB

text:
我为什么要设立孙宇晨奖

一
诺贝尔发明了炸药。他一生的财富，大部分来自这件东西。
据说1888年，一家法国报纸误发了他的讣告，标题叫"死亡商人死了"。他读到了自己的讣告，几年后立了遗嘱。
今天没有人再叫他死亡商人。
"诺贝尔"变成了一个中性的名词，像"伏特"和"瓦特"一样，不带感情，只是一个单位。他把钱交给"对人类做出最大贡献的人"，钱回到了人类手里，他的名字也随之回归中立，不是靠辩护，是靠一百多年的获奖名单。
我讲这个故事，是因为我理解他。我知道钱从哪里来，也知道钱可以去哪里。

二
我的财富，根源是数学。
区块链这个行业，整体建立在几个长期研究支撑的密码学构造与安全假设上：椭圆曲线上的离散对数难解，哈希函数不可逆，大数难以分解。1985年，两个数学家各自想到可以用椭圆曲线做密码，一个在大学，一个在IBM，互不相识。那年没有人觉得这件事有用。他们在黑板上写下的东西，后来变成了一个万亿美元的市场，变成了一种前所未有的东西——一个人可以完全支配自己的财富，不需要任何人许可。他们自己，一分钱没有拿到。
这种自由，是数学对人类最被低估的馈赠之一。我从这份馈赠里拿走了很多。设立这个奖，首先是还债。

三
诺贝尔奖没有数学奖。这是一百多年前的一个疏漏，也许有私人原因，也许只是没想到。
后来有了菲尔兹奖，四年一次，四十岁以下；有了阿贝尔奖，每年一次，奖励一生的成就。它们都很好，但它们的节奏，是上一个时代的节奏。
数学界其实有过另一种奖。Erdős一辈子给问题标价，从二十五美元到一万美元，谁解出来，他就开一张支票。很多人把支票裱在墙上，一辈子没有兑现。他1996年去世，之后那种支票开得越来越少。
而数学正在进入一个不同的时代。人工智能做不了实验，但它能推导；人工智能很难替物理学家造一台对撞机，但它可以替数学家试一万条路。今天一个猜想从提出到解决，可能是几个月，也可能是几天。一个四年颁一次的奖，面对这样的速度，像一座四年敲一次的钟，挂在一个以天计时的时代里。

四
所以孙宇晨奖的规则很简单。
奖跟着题目走，不跟着人走。不等年会，不等提名，不等年龄。
每道题，两栏署名。一栏记证明者，一栏记形式化者，把证明搬进机器的那个人。两栏可以是同一个人，也可以隔着半个地球互不相识。人可以，AI可以，人用AI也可以，哪一栏我都不关心物种。同一个名字可以一次又一次出现，出现在哪一栏都行。
钱只有一个触发器：机器把证明从第一行核到最后一行，一步不差。通过之后，两栏中的名单就是这道题的奖金所有者。这个标准不是我发明的。Scholze把自己最重要的定理挂出来，请人搬进机器；费马大定理，此刻正被人一行一行往里搬。
机器核过之前，人类的证明也不白做。数学界接受了，名字先挂上，钱一分不动，状态栏写着：已证明，待形式化。
解题那一栏的钱，只付给上架之后才被解决的题。上架时已经解决的，证明者的名字照记，钱只付给把它搬进机器的人。这个奖记录它设立之后发生的事，不给数学史补发奖金。
分工是干净的：名字归数学界，钱归机器，出资人两边都不沾。人的判断只剩一件事，确认写进机器的那道题，就是那道题。
还剩最后一件我说了算的事：题单。哪道题上架，开什么价，由我签字。Erdős的支票，价码也是他自己写的，这里不装例外。但货架一旦挂出，就锁死：题只加不减，钱只兑不退，包括我在内，谁也改不动。写错的题，照付，然后重挂。
我的品味，全部花在这一件事上。定价之外，验证、发钱、挂名，我一票都没有。
结果说了算。

五
这套规则里，我最喜欢的是一个"等"字。
一道题被解决、被数学界接受之后，钱不马上动。证明者的名字先挂上，形式化那一栏空着，状态栏写着：已证明，待形式化。谁把这份证明搬进机器，机器核过，空栏落上名字，钱的归属之旅也在那一刻启动。
在别的奖里，等是迟滞，是流程，是必要之恶。在这里，等本身是一份清单。
Erdős的支票，很多人裱在墙上，一辈子没有兑现。裱起来的钱朝后看，是纪念；挂在链上的钱朝前看，是召集。空在那里的一栏，等于对全世界说：这里有一份活，有价。
于是这份题单同时长出另一个东西：一张公开的地图，标着人类已经认下、机器还没有认下的一切。这张图今天并不存在。它只有碎片，散在几处，从来没有统一过，更从来没有带过价。
形式化的人从来不缺热情，缺的是一张带价码的施工图。谁去填那个空，谁拿钱。从今往后，把长证明搬进机器，热情还是他们的，账单归我。
author: sunyuchentron

text:
六
我还想说说品味。这是这个奖和诺贝尔奖真正分开的地方。
诺贝尔是发明家。他一生相信一件东西要有用，要落在地上，要造出来、卖出去、改变人的生活。这是他的品味，也刻在了他的奖里：物理、化学、医学、文学、和平，每一项都是对现实世界的奖励。一百多年来，这个奖奖励的是把楼盖在地上的人。
我的品味不同，而我不打算掩饰它的来源。我读过 Dario Amodei 的《慈爱的机器》（Machines of Loving Grace），深深赞同他在里面写下的那个画面：一个装在数据中心里的天才之国。
我之所以赞同，是因为我也在做同一件事。区块链从第一天起就是一个建在空中的王国：没有工厂，没有矿山，没有国土，只有共识和数学。我做人工智能，也是在往这个王国里添砖。我相信在这个世纪，人类最重要的建筑会有相当一部分建在空中，而空中王国的地基，只能是纯粹的推理。哈代1940年在《一个数学家的辩白》里写，他很欣慰数论这门学问永远不会有任何实际用途。八十年后，数论是我这个行业的地基。
所以我和诺贝尔选了不同的方向。他奖励落地的东西，我奖励悬空但严丝合缝的东西。这不是谁对谁错，是两个时代、两种品味。我想把这种空中王国的思想，用一个奖，一年一年地传下去。

七
2007年秋天，有三个人同一年进了北京大学。一个从深圳来，拿着奥数金牌，直接进了数学学院；一个从桂林来，先读的是地球与空间科学，后来转去了数学；一个从惠州来，读的是历史。
十九年后，前两个人在费城站上了同一个领奖台。王虹和邓煜拿到了2026年的菲尔兹奖。
第三个人是前段时间在飞机的卧室里，刷知乎刷到这条消息的。他把手机放下，第一个念头不是骄傲。是：我们这一代人，也到了该做点什么的时候了。
他们用证明做贡献。我不会证明。我能做的，是让证明的人拿到钱。

八
过去这些年，我做过不少零散的公益捐赠。从现在起，我的公益重心将转向这个奖。原因只有一个：这是我能为人类做的事里，贡献最大的一项。
奖目前只关注数学。

九
还有一件事：这个奖为什么叫我的名字。
两个原因。
第一，用人名命名的奖，是世上最不政治的东西。诺贝尔、菲尔兹、阿贝尔、图灵、沃尔夫，数学和科学界活得最久的奖，几乎都是一个人的名字。国家会变，机构会改名，公司会倒闭，一个人的名字一旦刻在奖上，就再没有人能修改它。
第二，是给我自己的一个交代。我三十六岁，积累的财富已经超过了我需要的量。一个人的财富如果没有方向，最后只会变成遗产纠纷和拍卖行的成交记录。我想趁自己还清醒的时候，亲手给这笔钱指一条路：它从数学来，回到数学去。
至于我自己的争议，名单是唯一的回答。我不要求任何人现在相信。
孙宇晨奖等得起。

十
最后一件事。这个奖不要求任何人信任任何人，你只需要相信机器的核验，而机器只认逻辑。首期奖池已经打入区块链，地址公开，余额全世界可见。我只保留了往里加钱的权利。
每一份获奖的证明都会公开，任何人都可以自己检验它是否成立，不需要相信我，也不需要相信任何委员会。每一笔奖金的发放都会留在链上，公开，不可更改，一百年后仍可查验。一个证明一旦成立，就永远成立；我希望对证明者的报偿，也是这种性质的东西。
我不是数学家。我是一个旁观者，我付钱。剩下的，交给证明。

孙宇晨

关于孙宇晨奖的更多信息，请访问以下官方渠道：

官网：https://t.co/HtvGGQGI81
