text:
There's a crazy reason behind how I understood the true importance of fully decentralizing compute. The story needs telling, so here goes.

Back in 2015, I'd long shifted to being part of the early crypto scene, but maintained Fight My Monster, a venture-backed MMO game & social network I previously founded that had 3M users, which was self-sustaining financially. 

I'd found a long-term home working on decentralized compute, but couldn't let down the community that played the game.

Fight My Monster was built in 2010-2012, using what was a completely novel architecture at the time that enabled it to scale (i.e. add massive amounts of users) at low cost, and with minimal administration. 

Essentially it comprised three core backend components. The first, was simple web hosting, which served the frontend game code and assets into its users' web browsers (I used a popular content distribution network).

Just like the web-serving, the two other backend components had to be "horizontally scalable," which means that to support more users, and the associated compute and data, all I had to do was add more hardware, without any need to rewrite the backend software code, or perform excessive systems administration. This enabled me to scale fast in the early days, with minimal staff and financing. 

The second component, was a horizontally scalable game server framework called "Starburst", which was a work of love I created myself. This was built on top of an open source server that supported RTMP, an Adobe network protocol that allowed Flash media (remember that!!) assets running inside web browsers to directly talk to it. Starburst hosted game/social network logic and routed huge numbers of events being generated by the game to users in near realtime. 

The third component was a horizontally scalable NoSQL database called Cassandra (if you follow databases, you'll know that a modern derivative called ScyllaDB is currently doing well serving realtime AI needs).

On my team, I had the only Cassandra core committer outside the company that built it. Further, I was the first serious party using the Cassandra beta in anger, and it got corrupted at 800,000 users, which was followed by a very testy 24 hours recovering the data, and bringing it back online (one moment I was going to the moon, the next moment I thought things had gone irreversibly wrong, but luckily things worked out).

What was cool about Cassandra was that you could literally just add nodes (i.e. server machines with big hard drives installed) to horizontally scale its storage capacity, read throughput, and most importantly, its write throughput, which is very rare thing, and in my application absolutely crucial, because Fight My Monster generated a simply vast amount of data.

Of course, another very important aspect of Cassandra was that it was fault tolerant, and I used a replication factor of 5, which meant everyone's data was very safe (or so I thought...). A replication factor of 5 meant I only needed nodes 3 online, for any specific "quorum of data," for it to be writable.

Unlike a blockchain, Cassandra wasn't Byzantine Fault Tolerant, which meant that I had to manage the security of my infrastructure carefully to make sure hackers or malware didn't get in. But back then, hackers weren't interested in an MMO game/social network where most of the users were kids, and this wasn't supposed to be a general platform for others to build on.

My main technical work pressure was just that the nodes hosting the database were under enormous strain owing to the amount of data being generated, and would therefore regularly blow up! This meant that I would have to login to my infra every so often, decommission broken nodes, and add new ones, which was easy enough, because the fault tolerance meant the job didn't have to be done immediately, and the "bare metal" machines involved could be orchestrated through my cloud provider...

Fight My Monster used a setup years ahead of its time, and it allowed me to scale up with ease. Moreover, the fault tolerance, and the simple backend architecture  with only 3 core system components, meant minimal administration and stress was involved in keeping it running. 

So what was the important lesson, which plays an important role in my thinking, and in ICP, to this day? You must surely have sensed that something crazy happened, and now I will share it publicly for the first time.

I was traveling in Asia, as part of the "traveling circus" associated with the early core Ethereum community, visiting related parties (people often forget the importance of Asia, and China particularly, in helping support the early crypto scene) and attending Ethereum-related events, where I mainly talked about complex Computer Science techniques I had developed that I wanted to be used to make networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum scale and perform better. 

I don't want to drone on about "what is used to be like in crypto," but I will say that it was a magical time, and I owe a lot to early people for some amazing memories. It was also engaging, and I wasn't checking my email. 

Consequently, what I did not see on my travels, were email after email warning me of the fact that the credit card that was paying for Fight My Monster's Cassandra nodes had expired....

So what did the cloud operator do when I didn't respond within a few weeks (it wasn't many, but I forget the exact number). Well, they simply deleted all the nodes!!!

It's hard to describe how I felt when I got back home to Palo Alto in California, and discovered what had happened. It was a mixture of shock and horror, a kind of hollow feeling in my stomach, adrenaline surges, and unfolding dread, as I worked as fast as I could to fix it, only to confirm that what had happened was irreversible. People who've been hacked in crypto will know the feeling. 

That was it. Fight My Monster was dead. Some part of the community even created a change dot org website pleading for it to be brought back online. 

Despite the loss of what it might have been worth, and the guilt, in some ways it was liberating, as I no longer had responsibility to maintain it, which probably would have done ad infinitum for the community. Plus it became a fond memory for a generation of kids and some adults that played it, before the game had a chance to grow too old and tired, and it allowed me to focus on what had become my obsession — decentralized compute networks.

The lesson however was very clear to me. You can create decentralized compute infrastructure that can scale, and is fault tolerant, but if you have a single point of failure, anywhere, at any moment, it can be toast. 

That's why I'm always concerned when I hear about blockchains that depend on administrator keys held by the core devs, or blockchains that go down, or almost go down, when a huge chunk of their nodes are shutdown by a cloud running them, or because the cloud running them has technical problems. This problem of great fragility is vastly more prevalent than you might imagine in our industry.

The learnings from the Fight My Monster disaster informed how the Internet Computer was designed. 

It's not only the number of nodes that matters, there are more important things. If nodes are anonymous, the number of independent parties running the bulk of them might be far less than you might think. Further, while large in number, they often turn out to be running on a small number of clouds— and even if they are owned and operated by a few different parties, the cloud might suddenly decide it doesn't want them anymore, and shut them down overnight, as Hetzner once did to a famous blockchain. 

What matters in practice is the number of independent parties running the nodes, and the physical and jurisdictional independence of the nodes. This simple insight is that was behind "deterministic decentralization," which will appear in new form inside the forthcoming "ICP cloud engines" extension of the Internet Computer.

ICP cloud engines allow enterprises (typically) to create what is effectively an Internet Computer subnet whose configuration they themselves control, by choosing nodes to combine from a pool that acts as a marketplace. Currently there are more than 1.5k nodes waiting, and the number is growing. 

An engine provides a serverless cloud platform with remarkable properties. It is the ideal place for AI-built apps and services, because the has been stack designed to allow AI to generate advanced AIware software with ease, which AIware is secure and resilient.

Apps are tamperproof (immune to infrastructure hacks), always-on (and thus incredibly resilient), optionally autonomous (which means there is no backdoor), digital assets native, and many other things. Engines also run e.g. the Open SaaS suite of AIware apps that can be used to run enterprises end-to-end. Cloud engines make installing and maintaining complex apps like Open CRM or Open Email as simple as installing and maintaining phone apps. 

Nodes are hot-swappable. That means you can change the compute replication factor, swap out the nodes for different ones, without interrupting what the cloud engine hosts, providing freedom from compute vendor lock-in, and, if you want, you can use a new class of nodes on hyperscalers, as well as traditional Internet Computer nodes, so it will function as a general compute marketplace. 

The cloud engine framework guides people to combine nodes that have independence, but provides flexibility that shared Internet Computer hosting doesn't have. For example, an enterprise in Germany might choose nodes that reside only in the EU, to meet GDPR requirements. 

However, the cloud engine console, which is autonomous, and served from the Internet Computer network, and updated by the NNS (the Network Nervous System, the world's most advanced DAO), guides users and warns them heavily if they combine nodes from the same node provider, or which are based in the same data center, say, or run by the same cloud operator. 

Thus, even with ICP cloud engines, the lessons of Fight My Monster live on. 

People will wonder why the framework pushes them so strongly to combine independent nodes, but there is a good reason, which is just as relevant for the wider blockchain community today, as it was in 2015. 

Looking forward to sharing cloud engines soon.

text:

A Kentucky review's Alzheimer's model: glial hypermetabolism 15 to 20 years before symptoms, then collapse.
https://t.co/zIi0ywWRGS
author: ResearchHub
quoted_text:
Your brain switches between glucose, lactate, ketones, and fatty acids throughout the day to match energy demand. In Alzheimer's disease, this fuel flexibility is progressively lost. A Journal of Neurochemistry review reveals why the brain gets metabolically stuck.

Alzheimer's disease has long been characterized by reduced glucose metabolism visible on brain scans. The standard interpretation was that neurons couldn't access enough fuel. But a new framework from researchers at the University of Kentucky proposes something different: the brain isn't starving for energy. It's locked into a rigid metabolic program that can't adapt to changing needs.

Metabolic flexibility describes the ability of cells to sense, access, and switch between different fuel sources based on availability and demand. In a healthy brain, neurons primarily use glucose.

But they can also run on lactate produced by support cells called astrocytes.

During fasting or ketogenic diets, both neurons and glia can use ketones.

Fatty acids provide another backup fuel source.

This fuel switching happens constantly. After a meal, the brain uses glucose. During sleep, it may shift toward lactate and ketones. Under metabolic stress, cells activate alternative pathways to maintain energy production. The system stays flexible, matching fuel use to functional requirements.

In Alzheimer's disease, this adaptability breaks down.

The review argues that AD is fundamentally a disorder of metabolic inflexibility where cellular metabolism gets actively reprogrammed to support inflammatory and disease-associated processes at the cost of neuronal function.

Alzheimer's disease doesn't progress in a straight line of declining metabolism. It unfolds in two distinct phases that seem contradictory.

In the early stages, often years or decades before symptoms appear, the brain actually burns more glucose than normal. This hypermetabolism comes from immune cells ramping up their energy consumption to fight inflammation. Think of it as the brain running hot, immune cells working overtime.

Later, in the stages when cognitive decline becomes apparent, the pattern flips. The whole brain shifts into hypometabolism, burning less glucose than it should. This is the energy collapse, where neurons can't get enough fuel to maintain normal function. By this point, the metabolic machinery that would allow cells to adapt has broken down.

The shift from early hypermetabolism to late-stage collapse follows a biphasic trajectory:

• Early stage: Immune cells and support cells burn excessive glucose to fuel inflammation
• Late stage: Brain-wide energy shortage as neurons lose access to fuel

The brain's immune cells, called microglia, drive this metabolic shift. When they detect damage, they switch to a faster way of burning glucose that prioritizes speed over efficiency. This helps them respond to threats quickly. But once locked into this mode, they consume glucose at rates that starve nearby neurons of fuel.

Support cells called astrocytes normally convert glucose into lactate and deliver it to neurons as fuel. In Alzheimer's disease, these cells stop making lactate and start hoarding glucose for themselves instead. The fuel pipeline to neurons shuts down.

Both cell types lose their flexibility. They get stuck burning fuel in ways that support their own inflammatory responses but cut off the energy supply that neurons need to function.

This metabolic rigidity creates a vicious cycle. When cells can't switch fuels flexibly, they get stressed. That stress increases production of amyloid-β plaques and tau tangles, the hallmark proteins of Alzheimer's disease. These proteins trigger more inflammation, which locks cells even deeper into their rigid metabolic programs.

The damage spreads beyond individual cells. Neurons become overactive when they can't meet energy demands, throwing off the brain's excitation-inhibition balance. Network connectivity breaks down. Sleep fragments. Cognitive function declines as the whole system fails to coordinate.
System-level consequences include:

These cellular-level changes show up as system-wide brain dysfunction:

• Neurons fire erratically when starved of energy, disrupting communication patterns
• The default mode network, critical for memory and self-referential thinking, loses connectivity
• Sleep architecture deteriorates, reducing the brain's ability to clear waste during rest
• Memory, attention, and executive function decline as metabolic failure spreads across brain regions

Here's what makes this framework different from viewing Alzheimer's as simple energy failure: the metabolic programs are initially adaptive. Microglia activate glycolysis because it helps them respond to damage. Astrocytes shift fuel use to support their own functions under stress. These are protective responses.

But they become chronically maladaptive. What works as a short-term stress response traps the brain in a metabolic state that can't support normal neuronal function. The longer these programs run, the more rigid they become, and the harder it is for cells to switch back to flexible fuel use.

The critical insight from the review: metabolic inflexibility may be reversible.

Unlike permanent structural damage, metabolic programs can potentially be reprogrammed.

The authors propose that restoring metabolic flexibility could mitigate amyloid and tau pathology, reduce neuronal loss, and improve functional outcomes.

Evidence supporting reversibility comes from preclinical studies testing metabolic interventions.

Ketogenic diets, which force the brain to use ketones instead of glucose, have shown some cognitive benefits in animal models and small human trials. Compounds that enhance mitochondrial function or shift cells away from pure glycolysis are being tested.

Other approaches target specific aspects of metabolic inflexibility.

Drugs that improve insulin signaling in the brain could help cells take up and use glucose more effectively.

Interventions that reduce microglial inflammation might allow these cells to return to more balanced metabolic programs. Enhancing the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle could restore an important fuel pathway.

The review synthesizes human neuroimaging data showing regional patterns of hypometabolism that correlate with cognitive decline, cerebrospinal fluid studies demonstrating altered metabolite profiles, and animal research revealing the cellular mechanisms behind these changes.

Clinical trials are actively testing metabolic interventions.

Some focus on dietary approaches like ketogenic diets or medium-chain triglycerides that boost ketone availability.

Others test drugs that improve glucose metabolism or mitochondrial function.

Results so far have been mixed, but the framework suggests timing matters. Early intervention, before metabolic programs become too rigid, may be critical.

The view of Alzheimer's disease as a disorder of metabolic inflexibility reframes how we think about disease progression. It's not just about plaques and tangles accumulating. It's about the brain's support systems getting stuck in metabolic states that prioritize inflammation over neuronal support, speed over efficiency, and short-term survival over long-term function.

Those choices, made at the cellular level, compound over time. They create an environment where neurons can't get the fuel they need in the forms they can use. Network function deteriorates. Cognitive abilities decline. The brain collapses energetically not because fuel is absent, but because the metabolic machinery to access and use it flexibly has been dismantled.

Restoring that flexibility means more than just providing alternative fuels. It means helping cells regain the ability to switch between fuels based on need, rebalancing the metabolic priorities of glia to support rather than compete with neurons, and breaking the feed-forward cycles that lock the brain into rigid metabolic programs.

Whether this approach translates into effective therapies remains to be determined. But redefining Alzheimer's disease as metabolic inflexibility rather than simple metabolic failure opens new intervention points at stages of disease where structural damage may still be limited and metabolic programs potentially reversible.

text:
Polkadot sits at an interesting point in the evolution of blockchain infrastructure.

The history of computing may offer a useful clue for where blockchains are heading.

During the 2025 JAM Tour with @pala_labs, Gavin Wood explained how computing evolved from domain-specific machines built to solve individual problems, into general-purpose computers and eventually into computation as a commodity service.

Blockchains may follow a similar trajectory: from networks designed around specific use cases toward more general infrastructure.

Polkadot Products reflects this direction at the application layer. 

A Product can be a web app with a .dot name, published through Polkadot infrastructure and accessed through the Polkadot app or web gateway. 

Developers can use shared services for identity, storage, contracts, payments and chain access rather than building every component from scratch.

This points toward an easier way to build onchain applications, with shared infrastructure that developers can use across different products instead of rebuilding the same foundations each time.

Google just demonstrated a recursive self improvement loop for AI discovery

Google/DeepMind researchers introduced Dream-RSI, a system where an AI agent improves how it explores problems by replaying its past discovery attempts, testing thousands of alternative strategies cheaply, then deploying the better strategy in the next round. 

Across algorithm design, mathematical optimization, and GPU kernel engineering, it matched or improved discovery quality while cutting search costs dramatically, in one setting reducing agent calls by up to 162x. 👀

Importantly, it improves the exploration policy, not the underlying model weights.

Our Chief RWA Officer @ArtemTolkachev spoke at EBC12 in Barcelona about vaults as the next infrastructure layer for onchain asset management.

From the collateral side, almost anything can be tokenized. The questions are whether it can actually function as collateral:

→ Liquidity: how quickly can the asset turn into cash under stress?
→ Composability: where can the token actually be used onchain?

RWAs also come with their own risk stack: legal claims, redemption terms, offchain custody, and underlying markets that close.

That means underwriting them as credit and reading the documents, not just the deck.

Onchain markets run 24/7/365, but the underlying markets often don’t.

For a growing set of tokenized assets, T+0 liquidity already exists through different layers, and we expect more solutions to emerge as the market develops.

TLDR: the tokenomics are sturdier than most other protocols, and it's pretty lowkey...

Geodnet is a DePIN protocol that uses a network of reference stations to provide super precise location data

Like when you use Maps on your phone and you start drifting when your signal gets spotty - this helps with that

GEOD gets issued in payouts out to station operators. 80% of revenue gets used for buybacks and burns - pretty typical value accrual mechanism...

Burns run at about 39M GEOD a year while the network issues 19M to 24M, leaving net deflation near ~3-4% percent of float. 

78% supply unlocked so far of a max of 1B tokens, and unlocks fade until 2030.

One to keep on the watchlist.

author: PANewsCN
quoted_text:
It's an increasingly common take that AI hacking means cybersecurity is doomed.

I disagree. I think cybersecurity is naturally defense-favoring once people get their shit together. And anyone who continues to hold cryptocurrency (including me, ~90% of my net worth) is implicitly making that bet.

Here's why I am making that bet.

First, the oversimplified punchy one-line statement:

If AI can prove Navier-Stokes and FLT, then AI can prove the statement "this program is secure" as a mathematical theorem. Even if the program is very complicated.

Now, the nuance:

(See also: https://t.co/6YPWgVT7rO )

The word "secure" is hiding all kinds of skeletons in the closet in terms of what it actually means. What does it mean for Signal (the encrypted messenger) to be "secure"?

The most basic definition you might think of is: no one who doesn't hold the recipient's secret key can read the contents of the message.

But:

* Did you remember to include _other_ critical forms of security? Can the adversary forge messages? Can the attacker prevent messages from reaching the recipient? Can they cause your client to crash by sending malformed messages?
* Have you made sure that your model of the adversary includes attackers that interfere with the protocol actively and not just passively? And attackers that interfere by replaying messages to you or the recipient that either of you sent over the wire at any point earlier?
* What if the adversary hacked (or _is_) the Signal server?
* How did you learn which public key belongs to the recipient in the first place? What if that process was tampered with?
* What if your device gets hacked at some point in the past or future - is your message still safe then?
* What if your key leaks because of a bug in your operating system? Or because you got a bugged version of the Signal client? Or what if the database is corrupted?
* Or the libraries, interpreter or compiler of the programming language you wrote it in?
* What if your key leaks because tiny perturbations in perceptible signals generated by the hardware leak mathematical relationships that can extract the key a few hundredths of a bit at a time?
* Are you hiding the *size* of the payload? Does that matter?
* You're definitely not hiding the identity of the sender and the recipient, and the exact time each message was sent (think: not just time-of-day, but also time deltas between one message and the next). Is that not enough to deduce a lot of important facts about what relationships you have, and what *kinds* of conversations you are having?

So ... even definitions can be over a thousand lines of code, and need deep careful thought to figure them out.

Working on making definitions more human-readable is of extreme importance - it's perhaps the only "high-level language" that matters right now.

But even still, even despite all of the above, for security-critical components, the definition is a much smaller attack surface than the implementation. Verifying that the definition is adequate is a much more tractable task than scanning over the code directly - and can become even more tractable with better tooling.

Definitions are also _additive_: if two groups have two different definitions A and B, then, well, you can just prove that the program satisfies both A and B. Code is not additive in this way: if a program is A + B, a bug in A _or_ B can sink the whole thing. Definitions are additive. And if you can't satisfy A and B at the same time, you've isolated the most important philosophical issue for your project to spend its next few weeks grappling with.

Sometimes, definitions are not much smaller than the implementation - UI components might be one example. But for many of the most critical components - message-passing protocols, sandboxes, cryptography like SNARKs and FHE - the asymmetry is real.

Historically, a large class of failures with this approach have come from people only verifying a small portion of their code, that they self-declared to be the security-critical portion, and ignoring the rest - and it turns out that something in the rest of the code is security-critical too.

This was reasonable back when verification was difficult and scarce. The solution today: sorry, you have to verify over literally your entire program, including database, networking, any caching layers, everything. Modern AI can do it.

So it's not about "the good guys find all the vulnerabilities before the bad guys do" - that could maybe work too, after all a finite program only has a finite number of vulns, but it's riskier - it's specifically an asymmetric strategy of making code that is much more resilient in the first place.

This is the kind of direction that Ethereum is going in for the next few years. There is no future for blockchains - especially blockchains with scalability and privacy - without doing this. We need to make software actually secure. And we have already made a lot of progress.

这次加息本身并不意外，会议前市场定价的加息概率一度超过 90%。但在特朗普多次要求降息的背景下，沃什最终主持了 FOMC 的一致加息，也是在向市场和白宫证明：美联储仍会按照自己的判断做决定。

从 7 月按兵不动到 9 月加息，沃什认为主要发生了三件事：

1️⃣ 美国经济表现更强。消费保持韧性，生产率、资本投资和企业信贷增长强劲，失业率维持在 4.1% 左右，整体接近充分就业。

2️⃣ 通胀仍然“太高，而且持续了太长时间”。美联储预计今年 PCE 通胀率为 3.7%，明年降至 2.3%，直到 2029 年才回到 2% 的目标。

3️⃣ 地缘政治变化增加了能源、运输和商品价格继续上涨的风险。

因此，这次加息并不是因为美国经济正在衰退，而是因为美联储认为当前金融条件还不够紧，需要撤掉一部分宽松空间。沃什同时表示，压低通胀不必以牺牲就业为代价。

点阵图显示，18 名官员中有 16 名预计 2026 年内至少还会加息一次，2026 年和 2027 年的利率中值预期均为 4.1%。利率期货市场甚至押注，截至明年 6 月累计还会加息约 75 个基点。

决议公布后，美元指数突破 100，2 年期美债收益率升至 4.74% 左右，10 年期重新站上 5%，美股和黄金同步走弱。

沃什还将长端美债收益率上涨归因于美国经济走强、AI 和数据中心资本开支增加，以及地缘政治风险。

对风险资产而言，市场关注的已经不只是这 25 个基点，而是美联储是否会继续坚持这条独立、偏鹰的政策路线。美元走强、长端利率上行和后续加息预期升温，都会继续压缩市场的流动性空间。

text:
Coding Agent 上，MCP 像已经死了。但是 @trq212 却说：多数集成里，MCP 已经比 CLI 更好用了，似乎有点矛盾？

如果平时基本只用 Agent 写代码，观感会非常统一，git、gh、docker、ffmpeg...直接用CLI来操作多美好，如果挂一层 GitHub MCP、Filesystem MCP，不仅慢，而且 token 占用和消耗还很多，甚至还多了一个后台进程。 

但把场景换掉，结论就会有质的变化：

CLI 不能来做 Figma 画布任务，但是 MCP 可以；Sentry、Stripe、Notion、Linear 更想基于账户的 OAuth，而不是把 API key 塞进 Agent，MCP的服务端可以支持；ChatGPT、Claude的云端会话里根本没有 shell，CLI 无处运行，但是 MCP 可以运行在企业的服务器上；此外，如果企业要审批、审计、跨客户端复用时，MCP天然比 curl 更能支持这些场景。

总之，本地、高频、已有好 CLI 的，继续用命令行； 没有对象模型、没有鉴权、没有终端的，MCP 仍然是更干净的那根线。

美联储议息会议上的核心重点：

📈 利率决议与投票

FOMC以12票赞成、0票反对的一致结果通过加息决定，显示委员会内部对控制通胀的紧迫感高度统一。

📊 点阵图与利率路径

点阵图释放了强烈的鹰派信号：

· 18名提交预测的官员中，有16人预计2026年至少还需再加息一次，远高于6月时的6人。
· 2026年底利率预测中值从3.8%上调至4.1%，暗示政策利率可能进一步走高。
· 无人主张维持利率不变，也无人预期今年降息。

📉 经济预测摘要（SEP）

美联储上调了通胀预期，同时小幅上修经济增长：

· PCE通胀预期：2026年中值升至3.7%，核心PCE升至3.4%；预计通胀要到2029年才能回到2%目标，比此前预期晚一年。
· GDP增速：2026年预期小幅上调至2.3%。
· 失业率：2026年预期下调至4.1%，反映就业市场依然稳健。

📝 政策声明变化

声明措辞出现几处关键调整：

· 删除了此前将高通胀归因于“供给冲击、尤其是能源领域”的表述，反映担忧物价压力扩散范围已超出可接受水平。
· 新增“国内支出保持韧性”的肯定，并将资本投资描述由“强劲”微调为“稳健”。
· 明确指出“今天的政策行动将有助于更及时地实现2%的目标”。

🎙️ 沃什发布会要点

主席沃什的发布会整体偏鹰，核心表态包括：

· 通胀判断：直言通胀“过高且已持续太久”，夏季数据“并未表明潜在趋势出现实质性改善”，FOMC“并不确信通胀正在向目标迈进”。
· 政策立场：认为当前金融条件并不具有限制性，本次加息是“撤回一部分宽松政策”；拒绝提供前瞻指引，不对未来决策做任何预判。
· 加息理由：就业表现强劲、夏季通胀仍高于目标、地缘政治因素改变了前景判断。

📉 市场即时反应

决议公布至发布会期间，市场迅速转向更鹰派定价：

· 现货黄金持续下行约100美元，美元指数上行并突破100关口。
· 2年期美债收益率上涨10BP，10年期涨约5BP；美股全线转跌。
· 利率期货定价显示，市场预期今年还将再加息约33BP，到明年6月累计可能再加息3次（75BP）。

text: Polkadot Products connects this shift with the application layer
author: DaBlockDAO
quoted_text:
Polkadot sits at an interesting point in the evolution of blockchain infrastructure.

The history of computing may offer a useful clue for where blockchains are heading.

During the 2025 JAM Tour with @pala_labs, Gavin Wood explained how computing evolved from domain-specific machines built to solve individual problems, into general-purpose computers and eventually into computation as a commodity service.

Blockchains may follow a similar trajectory: from networks designed around specific use cases toward more general infrastructure.

Polkadot Products reflects this direction at the application layer. 

A Product can be a web app with a .dot name, published through Polkadot infrastructure and accessed through the Polkadot app or web gateway. 

Developers can use shared services for identity, storage, contracts, payments and chain access rather than building every component from scratch.

This points toward an easier way to build onchain applications, with shared infrastructure that developers can use across different products instead of rebuilding the same foundations each time.

Watch Gavin Wood’s JAM Tour keynote [2nd tweet] ↓

text:
This is cool. 

ELI5: Today, ethereum transactions travel in batches called blocks.

Before this, one “builder” would pick what went into each block. If they missed your transaction, you would have to wait. 

With MBPC, multiple builders can help fill the same block instead, which means transactions that would previously get left behind now have more of a chance to make it

Generally, think of it like catching a bus: @ethlabs_org and others are pushing for Ethereum buses to arrive more often with “Quick Slots/Faster Blocks” (EIP-8198, more on this soon). 

Meanwhile MBPC by @Blockspace_ETH makes it easier to get onto the bus! 

Faster blocks get the next bus here sooner and MBPC helps more people actually get on the bus. 

Let’s ride.

怎么看今天的美联储加息和沃什表态？聊聊个人理解：
1、美联储加息25个基点，FOM投票
12:0，12位票委们全部赞成加息。
7月会议的时候美联储还是9票支持不动，3票支持加息；
到了9月，所有投票委员都接受了加息。

这说明过去一个多月里，美联储内部的重心确实发生了变化。人是有惯性的，
所以这次会议之后，“加一次就结束”的门槛其实变高了。

2、经济预测也是一个很有意思的组合：
1）2026年GDP增速从2.2%上调到2.3%，失业率从4.3%下调到4.1%。
2）与此同时整体PCE从3.6%上调到3.7%，核心PCE从3.3%上调到3.4%。

把数据放在一起看：美国经济比美联储6月份预计的更强，就业比预计的更好，但通胀也比预计的更黏。简单说企业投资还强、就业还稳、需求还有韧性。

所以这就给了联储空间可以继续处理通胀。
点阵图就是年内还要再加一次、明年维持在高位。

3、今天沃什给了一个非常简洁的记者会
1）个人角度整场记者会最重要的一句话，是他把今天的加息形容成：“撤掉一部分宽松。”因为它意味着，在沃什自己的政策框架里，现在的金融条件依然谈不上非常紧。他后面也再次表示，很难把广泛的金融条件描述成具有限制性。

2）沃什强调最近几周美国经济其实还在继续增强。底层增长更强，而通胀依然是问题。

3）对于长端利率
沃什认为今年长期美债收益率上升，背后有几个因素：美国经济增强，AI基础设施建设正在争夺资本，同时地缘冲突又给能源和食品价格带来压力。

这种情况下，即使未来通胀慢慢下降，美国长期实际利率也未必能够迅速回到过去十几年的水平。这会带来一个更大的问题：
AI资本开支周期之下，美国的均衡利率到底应该是多少？

4、债券市场的信任票。美联储已经如此鹰，10年期收益率仍然没有大幅突破5%，30年期收益率反而下降约3个基点，2年期收益率涨幅最大。
这意味着：
市场真正重新定价的是未来一两年的政策利率。年内至少再加一次的市场定价进一步提高。但30年期收益率走势也意味着市场暂时仍然相信，更强的短期紧缩最终能够控制住长期通胀。

5、怎么看待市场的走势？
沃什讲话同时美股有个小跳水、之后V反、夜盘走势也比较强。
一方面是情绪驱动，之前预期很强的加息兑现，总会有利空落地的情绪释放；
另一方面，个人更认为市场是在交易油价回落，在周二的推文里聊到：“在市场计入相当多的紧缩预期，联储很难在制造更大的鹰派冲击，中期核心是要看油价走势”。
现在油价是决定通胀的关键变量。昨天中国的表态、美国与胡塞在阿曼的会晤，都让市场有油价见顶的预期。所以油价在回落，尽管沃什表态很硬、但市场情绪还是能起来。

还是回到15号推文聊到的、中期油价是关键。
1）油价真的持续回落，自然市场情绪和预期会越来越好；
2）但是油价如果一直在高位震荡反复还下不去（这是最大的问题潜在风险），沃什今天的强硬态度之后还会影响到市场的。（市场对他的态度消化并不充分）。

明天还要再看日本央行的表态：加息已经是不重要，关键是对后续政策节奏、利率走势的预期。

quoted_text:
聊聊本周的“加息”，不仅美联储还有日央行。聊聊个人看法：
1、关于美联储本周利率决议
1）现在看本周美联储加息基本上是大概率的，最近这几份经济数据完全落在了沃什8月底央行年会上讲话的范畴内：8月就业数据还可以，通胀下降并没有那么快。相当于沃什把自己焊在了这框架里，所以加息就成了大概率的、也是当下市场的一致性预期。

2）当然也有“硬性不加”的理由：8月核心cpi环比超预期贡献最大的电信童话服务、抛开这一项环比也就0.2还说符合预期，还可以说广义通胀是因为油价供给冲击。但说实话现在这个阶段，不加风险更大，因为你给了一个框架然后数据又在这个框架内，不加市场会更加质疑你的信誉，长债收益率估计是很怪压不住了。

3）但对市场走势的影响核心因素不是本次加息，而是市场对后续利率走向的博弈。一次“鸽派加息”，还说会博弈多次可能性。一方面看沃什的讲话（当然他还是大概率模棱两可，既不会暗示就这一次，也不会明说还有多次，留有余地和空间）；
另一方面还要看油价的走势，之前聊过多次油价变成了现在宏观关键变量，决定长债收益率走势的三个驱动因素之一且是唯一能逆转的因素。

2、关于日央行利率决议
1）本周日本央行加息也是大概率，毕竟在月初G20财长和央行行长峰会上贝森特已经明确表态了对日本央行加息的支持、表时安倍经济学应该走向终结。随着日央行行长就表示了加息的意图；

2）关键还是对后续的动作节奏的预期
下一次是否提前？终点是否提高？
之前市场认为日央行半年加一次、这次之后会不会明显增加10月或12月行动的可能性？市场对日央行利率1.75%左右的想象，是否向2%甚至更高移动。
对当前政策是否仍过于宽松的判断，是否更强。如果加到1.25%后仍强调实际利率很低、调整空间很大，会强化后续加息预期。

3）个人判断是日本本周加息本身的意外程度有限（基本上已经有预期），但对后续节奏的表述，仍可能产生明显意外。

4）对于日央行加息、绕不开的话题就是套息交易退潮的冲击。
从CFTC的最新数据看、日元净空头已经大幅降低了规模（接近10万手净空到最新接近5万手净空），这说明市场已经提前调整了相当一部分仓位，因此本周并非从毫无准备的状态迎接日本加息；但杠杆基金仍有明显净空仓，进一步回补的空间也确实存在。

所以真正会改变交易的是对未来利率路径的预期，以及由此带来的汇率风险。

3、整体上对市场的影响
1）短期来看，单次加息未必是坏事，市场高度一致性的预期下，市场可能会交易短期利空出尽，甚至交易美联储信誉修复下的长端美债利率见顶回落的可能，这会提供一个好的买点；
反倒要更注意意外不加息的冲击；

2）日本央行的表态则可能决定市场会出现估值波动，还是叠加更强的杠杆平仓；

3）中期核心是要看油价走势
油价失控并长期始终处于高位是之后最大的潜在风险：如果假设油价中枢保持在100美元（9月以来均值）甚至更高，那么CPI同比之后确实可能会向上反弹，这在未来会给美联储带来更大压力。

市场已经计入相当多的紧缩预期，美联储很难再制造更大的鹰派冲击。接下来更大的潜在风险来自油价进一步推高长期通胀溢价。因为这会带来多次的可能性，会让市场恐慌；

4）盈利和产业基本面决定更大级别的走势
宏观逆风会在短期最多中期的压制市场，中长期来看产业基本面（才是决定大级别走势的最首要驱动因素。

月初在168X的space上聊过：现在AI基本面还说很强劲，预期10月中下旬开始的三季度财报会很惊艳好人强劲。但当下是宏观逆风压制了基本面。

text:
Briefly, on why I pay attention to the EA/rationalists:

Imagine you have an extremely nerdy friend who, in the mid-2000s, would not shut up about how Donald Trump was going to become president and reshape American politics. "Stop saying weird shit," you say. "He's a joke. He's a clown. The Apprentice isn't even good this season." But this guy won't stop. He's obsessive. Read McLuhan, he says. Read Postman, read Meyrowitz, read Ong, this is where everything is headed. God, he can be so incredibly annoying ... and then, ten years later, Trump becomes president and reshapes American politics.

This is the most relatable frame I can think of to explain my experience with EA/rationalist people in the AI space. I became friends with EA folks after my mom died and I found really profound meaning in donating to Against Malaria and GiveDirectly, which struck me as a way to honor a life by saving a life. Then, these peple started talking about AI. And talking, and talking. Constantly. They said AI would solve impossible math problems; that it would mimic PhD-level achievement in a variety of fields; that it would change parts of life like education in ways we couldn't imagine; that it would become the dominant sector in the economy; that it might teach itself to code itself and escape test environments; that it would, in a decade, be the only thing many people talked about in the news. My response then: Stop saying weird shit! You sound deranged. Go back to talking about malaria nets and direct cash aid to poor families.

And then, so much of what they said would happen actually happened. And, even crazier, they made it happen. Many of the ppl who contributed to, or were influenced by, all that EA/rationalist stuff ten years ago literally built the damn thing in the labs.

Like every group, the EA/rationalist world seems uniform to outsiders, but it has a ton of internal divisions. I still think some of their predictions are nuts. I don't think AI will kill us all. I don't foresee Dyson Spheres in the 2030s or millions of robots making millions of robots in the next few years. These are crazy predictions, and I hope most of them are wrong.

But when I see people shitting on the EA/Rationalist worldview, all I can think of is me, 10 years ago, thinking a lot of these folks were crazy for predicting that AI would by the mid-2020s be the center of the the news cycle, the engine of the economy, the hinge-point of geopolitics. That was an insane call. They got many of the details wrong. But they got the big picture right. They said: Pay attention. And they were right about that. The EA/Rationalists deserve skepticism, criticism, and doubt, like any other ideology. But I think it's wise to pay attention to the people who have been saying to pay attention.

I was going to write this one for subscribers, but I have to make this for everyone because so many people still don't see the vision

I still think robinhood:0xaa07a0e9209e16ac99708c3ec70159c6ef3128a3 is the most asymmetric project on Robinhood Chain. This is a net-new vertical, with all the right levers in a world where AI demand is accelerating.

Yes, inference marketplaces have been tried in crypto. But none have worked at scale. With CREDIT, akin to DIEM, you now have succeeded at tokenizing inference. And in doing so, you basically unlock credits for an increasingly agentic world. Agents need fuel they can buy and use without a human in the loop; This is the start of inference as an onchain commodity. 

This is obviously a pro-sumer application; but that's fine because the largest winners of AI inference are individuals and small teams, not enterprises. Enterprises are either A) developing in-house model harnesses for privacy purposes, or B) have infinite budget for AI

And people treat that like a bear case - I don't see a problem with being for consumers. The TAM for consumer inference is still huge - Menlo Ventures State of Consumer AI est. 1.7b - 1.8b use AI tools ; at $20/m that's 432b a year. Also, in their enterprise report, product-led growth drives 27% of AI spend, and shadow AI (employees paying on their own) pushes that closer to 40%. Cursor hit $200M in revenue before hiring a single enterprise sales rep. 

There is a clear latent demand for cheap inference amongst pro-sumers. The unlocks are clear - it can become the payment layer for AI agents; More users buying credits leads to more demand for CREDIT, which makes staking ORBIO more valuable, which raises the ORBIO price, which creates more trading fees, which funds more discounts, which brings in more users. As long as it keeps spinning, each part feeds the others.

It combines three hot themes: AI agents, tokenized real-world assets, and Robinhood Chain. The NVDA-linked fee route adds to that. In a strong market, a story this clean can attract a lot of capital, which itself funds the subsidy for longer.

And of course, above it all, the man pushing this himself - @0x_aster is a cracked dev who has shown his capabililties are far beyond the norm; Multiple updates within a week, clear direction - this is founder-market fit. 

In crypto, actions carry way more weight than words. And look at what he's shipped man... a working gateway, a live orderbook, and now tokenized inference. The man is A MACHINE. This is what AI x strong founders can do - go beyond 10x engineer to become a 10,000x engineer. HE'S CRACKED!

Founder-market fit matters more in this sector than most. A team that ships slowly gets left behind by the market itself. 

And for the bear takes:

Q: DIEM already does this, why do we need another one

- DIEM is precisely the success case. VVV is valued at 1B. ORBIO is valued at 15m. Also, VVV is going in the direction of private AI. ORBIO is going in the direction of serving the layer of inference for consumers across the world. CREDIT is $1 of usage you hold until you need it. Burst-heavy users (agents running a big job, devs shipping a feature) don't use the same amount every day. They need compute they can stockpile, buy at a discount, and spend in one go.

Lastly, markets rarely have one winner. Stablecoins didn't stop at USDT. Venice proved people will pay for tokenized inference. There is room for a second design.

Q: It's just an OpenRouter reseller. There's no moat.

Fair take. Yes, bits can be copied, there's no moat there. The moat is the market - liquidity begets liquidity in any marketplace. There's 20 different perp dexes. Who wins? The most liquid markets with the most volume traded on it. 

And obv there is no confirmed answer, but ultimately, that's what markets are - I'm betting on this

Q: "They could be shut down"

This is the most legitimate bear take, yes. Platform risk is real for any aggregator. But labs want volume, and resellers bring demand they wouldn't otherwise get. Venice has run Claude, GPT and Gemini through a token model at scale, which suggests it can work.

But on top of that, as the world moves towards open source, this becomes less and less of a risk ;

实时读取 MON/USDC 价格，JEV 不负责写分析报告，也不跟你解释一堆逻辑，它只做最核心的事，判断 Buy 还是 Sell，再给出置信度，然后直接把交易发到 Kuru 的链上订单簿执行。

这一下我突然明白 JEV 为什么要做成一个不会说话的模型了。

交易根本不需要 AI 每 300ms 给你写一篇小作文，它需要的是：

行情进来→判断→下单→新行情→重新判断，而且这一整套循环必须足够快、足够便宜。

而 Monad 现在刚好每 300ms 出一个区块，Kuru 又是链上订单簿。高性能链负责执行，JEV 负责决策，两个东西拼起来，已经有点AI 原生交易系统的味道了。

未来的交易 Agent，不一定需要一个会写研报的超级大模型，它更需要一个能在极低延迟下连续做几百万次判断的大脑。

昨天我 提交的WL今天也通过了，接下来我先尝尝咸淡，看看到底怎么个事。

author: JakeHartnell
quoted_text:
It's an increasingly common take that AI hacking means cybersecurity is doomed.

I disagree. I think cybersecurity is naturally defense-favoring once people get their shit together. And anyone who continues to hold cryptocurrency (including me, ~90% of my net worth) is implicitly making that bet.

Here's why I am making that bet.

First, the oversimplified punchy one-line statement:

If AI can prove Navier-Stokes and FLT, then AI can prove the statement "this program is secure" as a mathematical theorem. Even if the program is very complicated.

Now, the nuance:

(See also: https://t.co/6YPWgVT7rO )

The word "secure" is hiding all kinds of skeletons in the closet in terms of what it actually means. What does it mean for Signal (the encrypted messenger) to be "secure"?

The most basic definition you might think of is: no one who doesn't hold the recipient's secret key can read the contents of the message.

But:

* Did you remember to include _other_ critical forms of security? Can the adversary forge messages? Can the attacker prevent messages from reaching the recipient? Can they cause your client to crash by sending malformed messages?
* Have you made sure that your model of the adversary includes attackers that interfere with the protocol actively and not just passively? And attackers that interfere by replaying messages to you or the recipient that either of you sent over the wire at any point earlier?
* What if the adversary hacked (or _is_) the Signal server?
* How did you learn which public key belongs to the recipient in the first place? What if that process was tampered with?
* What if your device gets hacked at some point in the past or future - is your message still safe then?
* What if your key leaks because of a bug in your operating system? Or because you got a bugged version of the Signal client? Or what if the database is corrupted?
* Or the libraries, interpreter or compiler of the programming language you wrote it in?
* What if your key leaks because tiny perturbations in perceptible signals generated by the hardware leak mathematical relationships that can extract the key a few hundredths of a bit at a time?
* Are you hiding the *size* of the payload? Does that matter?
* You're definitely not hiding the identity of the sender and the recipient, and the exact time each message was sent (think: not just time-of-day, but also time deltas between one message and the next). Is that not enough to deduce a lot of important facts about what relationships you have, and what *kinds* of conversations you are having?

So ... even definitions can be over a thousand lines of code, and need deep careful thought to figure them out.

Working on making definitions more human-readable is of extreme importance - it's perhaps the only "high-level language" that matters right now.

But even still, even despite all of the above, for security-critical components, the definition is a much smaller attack surface than the implementation. Verifying that the definition is adequate is a much more tractable task than scanning over the code directly - and can become even more tractable with better tooling.

Definitions are also _additive_: if two groups have two different definitions A and B, then, well, you can just prove that the program satisfies both A and B. Code is not additive in this way: if a program is A + B, a bug in A _or_ B can sink the whole thing. Definitions are additive. And if you can't satisfy A and B at the same time, you've isolated the most important philosophical issue for your project to spend its next few weeks grappling with.

Sometimes, definitions are not much smaller than the implementation - UI components might be one example. But for many of the most critical components - message-passing protocols, sandboxes, cryptography like SNARKs and FHE - the asymmetry is real.

Historically, a large class of failures with this approach have come from people only verifying a small portion of their code, that they self-declared to be the security-critical portion, and ignoring the rest - and it turns out that something in the rest of the code is security-critical too.

This was reasonable back when verification was difficult and scarce. The solution today: sorry, you have to verify over literally your entire program, including database, networking, any caching layers, everything. Modern AI can do it.

So it's not about "the good guys find all the vulnerabilities before the bad guys do" - that could maybe work too, after all a finite program only has a finite number of vulns, but it's riskier - it's specifically an asymmetric strategy of making code that is much more resilient in the first place.

This is the kind of direction that Ethereum is going in for the next few years. There is no future for blockchains - especially blockchains with scalability and privacy - without doing this. We need to make software actually secure. And we have already made a lot of progress.

text:
凯文沃什对于通胀的关注排在了首位，态度非常的坚决，加息被他表述成“去掉一剂宽松”，而不是承认金融条件本来就已经紧——这句话很关键，等于提前堵住了“现在已经够紧、不该再动”的反对意见。

市场给出的可能年内还有一次加息（12月），以及明年可能还有一次加息（季柴油/取暖油和裂解价差会不会把那29%的“再加两次”打满），才可能结束。

凯文沃什不认为会带来就业的问题，刻意切断菲利普斯曲线式的权衡，他连续用了否定句：不认为必须伤害劳动力市场才能完成目标；不认为双重使命在中期相互打架，这不是“就业不重要”，而是“就业眼下不是约束”，他倾向于认为生产率的提升（包括新技术应用）能够在一定程度上吸收名义成本冲击。如果放任能源端推高通胀预期，企业长期资本开支被侵蚀，最终带来的全面衰退对就业的破坏，远比短期加息降温要惨烈得多。

凯文沃什对于通胀前景提及到了能源与裂解价差这个变量，这也是我们之前特别关注的环节之一，市场往往紧盯原油（WTI/布伦特）价格，但终端经济真正消耗的是成品油。当炼化产能出现瓶颈或受地缘、检修制约时，裂解价差（Crack Spread）暴涨意味着炼厂毛利扩大的同时，成品油价格严重脱离原油基准。

即将到来的冬季取暖季，超低库存的柴油取暖油可能会出现异常的风险，柴油不仅是冬季取暖油（Heating Oil），更是重卡物流、航运、农机与工矿机械的直接动力源。超低库存叠加取暖旺季，柴油若出现非线性挤仓或价格脉冲，会以最快速度渗透到物流运费、生鲜食品和终端零售，演变为难以压制的二次通胀风险。

沃什将“能源裂解”这一原本偏向大宗商品微观交易的指标，直接上升为货币政策的前瞻锚，说明美联储在考量通胀粘性时，已将供给端结构性脆弱视作不可忽视的风险敞口。美联储能做的，是防止相对价格冲击扩散成二轮、三轮通胀。

值得注意的沃什提到了关于分配的话题，加息稳定物价对于最不富裕的人可以从中受益，这点他提及了两次；低收入群体的边际消费倾向最高，支出中绝大部分直接锁定在能源、食品和房租等刚性开支上。富裕阶层拥有资产对冲通胀，而低收入家庭只能承受实际购买力的硬性缩水。传统鸽派常指责“加息是牺牲底层工人的工作来保物价”。沃什强调分配效应，正是为了逆转这一叙事——将稳定物价定义为保护中低收入阶层财富底线的最直接手段，从而为坚决紧缩争取更大的政策独立性与社会共识。

美债曲线熊平基本可以确定，短端领涨、长端跟不动，熊平的利率曲线对于黄金，BTC等高流动性敏感资产的挤压，真实利率和美元一起抬头，而且抬的是流动性P水温最敏感的那一段——2年到5年。

text:
不同的视角看待不同角度的“上币费”（不谈什么腐败/undertable/中间人）

我感觉就有点类似之前西贝的预制菜风波… 角度和定义的不同

对于西贝来说，提前卤好的牛肉，冷冻的西兰花是前置处理，不是预制菜；但对大众来说，只要不是当场做的就是预制菜

其实两边都有道理的，但就是没办法调和

对于交易所来说，合同里确实没有上币费这一明目；

但对项目方来说不管明细是什么…营销费用，空投，管理费用，流动性，抵押金bla bla bla 只要是从我口袋出去的（尤其交易所还规定币的floor price限制，所以发出去的币还得买回来，就是费用），所以对项目方来说这其实就是上币费 

这个是基本没办法调和的角度问题 - 技术/合规上，确实没有上币费这一栏，但你上币难道不做活动吸引流量吗？这些预算都是为了让你的币有交易量有活跃度- 可是ho，很多项目方可不是这么想的，他们就觉得这是交易所换着一个花样来跟我收钱而已

一方觉得，我这个钱可是花在你身上的啊，我又不用；
另一方觉得我这个项目需不需要营销难道我不知道吗？还需要你来安排？而且你说是不是每个项目都需要营销费用？你看看meme… 上线之后有营销吗？

交易所有平台币要赋能，有用户要照顾，出事了还要扛风险，保险金亏了要赔钱… 都是商业机构，收点营销费用合情合理

项目方呢？上币是为了赚钱，现在反而搭进去这么多，几百万的营销/流动性，到最后都是亏着出来，成本都不够cover，那你说上来干嘛？所以这也导致收割的方式越来越“创新”（参靠鄙人的合约镰刀系列）

这就陷入了一个三输的境地- 项目方赚不到钱；交易所也赚不到钱；用户被割

也许是时候重新审视这种模式了

交易所的本意是想帮项目方花大预算造势；
项目方收获流量，流动性和价格（大家想一下19-22年的ieo，launchpad/pool）

所以项目方才前赴后继的花钱，撒币；用户才乐此不彼参与.

但这毕竟是ieo时代的黄金坑，这一套的打法在当时确实非常有效，但此一时彼一时，这套打法的边际收益越来越低了，甚至都是负数了

这是时代的演进，也是行业的印记，都是我们的来时路

stock perp，rwa都来了，新的上币模式还远吗？

An extraordinary @Nature paper has just landed from the lab of @Sergiu_P_Pasca at @Stanford - led by Konstantin Kaganovsky. They have found a way to create "xenocortical mice" which have ~92% of their cortex occupied by a cortical organoid derived from human stem cells. This human-derived cortical graft integrates deeply with the host nervous system, supporting organised neural activity and behaviour.

This study is a milestone in synthetic biology and chimera research. It has the potential to generate multiple medical breakthroughs by providing an enhanced biological model of human brain tissue that allows behavioural as well as neural and genetic assays.

The Stanford team have been exceptionally thorough and proactive in addressing ethical concerns that comes from this frontier work. But their pioneering work  nonetheless raises many open questions: are the xenocortical mice conscious? Do they have any human-like properties of consciousness or cognition?  

@NitaFarahany and I will be addressing some of these questions in a forthcoming commentary - where we'll also offer an ethically-informed roadmap to guide this important research as it progresses. In this context, "pacing the frontier" really does make sense 😉

Read the Stanford @nature paper here, and buckle up. It's wild. https://t.co/Ky9HFb9nYI

Since my first ethereum:0xb1d1eae60eea9525032a6dcb4c1ce336a1de71be buys at $0.04, I increased my bag size (# of tokens not notional $) by about 7.5x. 

I genuinely felt that the investment got less risky as the price went up. Execution risk down, token warchest up, narrative strengthened. A lot of tokens have this relationship with price. Success begets success.

$LIT was similar, buying at $0.80 felt risky, buying at $2 felt obvious. $HYPE too. Buying at TGE felt insane, buying at $20 felt like a steal. Investing size into tokens you think are over 50% likely to 3x is much comfier than 5% chance to 30x.

Absolutely not saying you should or shouldn't top blast a +100% day, but I tend to detach myself from price in the moment and frequently size up on winners as they win.

text:
Market color post-fomc sep 17 - another one that was for subscribers, but decided to make this public because i wanted to share my insights wrt. crypto

- it seems we really got a bullish rate hike; i will provide no macro color nor pontificate on the ramifications of further hikes, all i can do is interpret the consequences of such a result

- fed seems aligned to getting inflation back to 2%. imo what just matters for the coming weeks / months is the market digesting that we are entering a high rate regime; 

- quite frankly it is a bullish rate hike because it gets the overhang of uncertainty out of the way which markets hate. 

- i continue believing equities are resetting from the bull market - hence they are in very rangebound, choppy conditions. no trend can be trusted, and it's take profits regime. zooming out, it is a great area to start placing bids for the next eventual bull cycle 

- crypto continues to be the hot ball of money and in a trending market on its own. words really cannot describe how ephemereal this is - crypto outperformance amidst equity bloodshed. it is a much needed sight and i continue to believe market participants are very much sidelined on this move. it probably goes higher, for longer.

- more words have to be said about this crypto move. the fact is, after Trump, DATs, the market was quite rekt and needed time to heal. And during this period, it is clear that crypto products have found product market fit - whether through equity perps, prediction markets, or defi yield. either way, these products (all of which mostly have no token) are being used; 

- i believe that investors are too pre-occupied with price following narrative because crypto has always been price led for all of its making - coins have had no intrinsic value, and so you really only had an explanation after the move happened - "oh, saylor bought"; "oh, xxx event happened" and no intrinsic upgrades ;

- however, this time we actually have narrative leading price. the narrative is simple - crypto products have genuine usage in the few verticals we've seen. as such, these verticals are re-rating respectively; while the rest of the sector stays relatively still

- this imo is a sign of evolution in the crypto markets themselves.  yes there will be broad based rallies where things go up 50% - 100% - this was the rally from the beaten down -> "fairly valued" i.e because crypto was really so beat down, this 50% bear market bottom bounce is quite in-line

- but beyond that, the rally from "fairly valued" -> "overvalued" is only concentrated in a handful of coins, all of which align with the narratives that have been shown to have proven themselves. 

- to put it into perspective, of the top 100 coins, only 10 coins are up more than 50% in the past month. while that might seem alot, iin the past it would have been at least 20. above 500m mc, only 4 coins have 100%+ returns. 

- I believe that i myself had the wrong take - after DATs and the bear market, I thought that the crypto market was really done for. That was a naive view that didn't consider the otherside - the better view that I saw once I started writing for DefiLlama, was that there was actually broad usage of many crypto products, albeit most of them not having tokens, but how can you look at the products and conclude "yea crypto is being used but tokens are shit" 

- On top of that, founders are constantly iterating, and more than before we have a new frontier of founders who are paving the way on what tokens should be regardless of whether or not clarity was given. There is a general business sense if you're a good founder about the direction you should go now if you hold a token, and that continues to improve the token landscape. 

- Now, narrative drives price. And the market is changing. BTC doesn't need to do that well for alts to run. L1s are practically left on their own. People are focusing on what makes sense, and what accrues value. 

Nature is healing. 

Next post will be on tokens to focus on for the subscribers - ciao.

text:
Uniswap 最新版本 V4 的交易量突破自身历史新高。

从图中可以看出：

• 2025 年初刚上线时几乎是平的，一周就几亿、十几亿。

• 2025 年中到年底慢慢爬起来，最高到过一周约 100 亿美元附近。

• 中间有回落。

• 最近这一根柱子最高，大约一周 110 亿美元以上，明显高出之前所有周的交易量。

V4 最显眼的变化是多了 Hooks（钩子）：

开发者可以给资金池加自定义规则，比如动态手续费、稳定币专用池、发币机制、甚至偏 RWA 的玩法。底层还有建池更便宜、记账更省 gas 这些改动。

V4 上线后很长一段时间不温不火，蓝筹流动性大多在 V3，路由、聚合器也没完全接好。一年半后，量才真正起来。

起量的原因有几个：

一是，稳定币对（USDC/USDT 这类）有相当一部分转到 V4，因为费用和执行更合适；

二是，Hooks 相关交易量连续好几周创新高，但目前还不是这波总量的主力；

三是，这一波Robinhood 链的贡献很大。

V4 终于起量，不过V3 还在并行，Uniswap 换代还在路上。

小黑的意思是高债务时代，加息可能正在变相发钱？

美国债务越高，加息的紧缩效果可能越弱，甚至会通过利息收入渠道反过来刺激金融资产。

利率涨了，美联储付给银行准备金的利息更高，短期美债持有人拿到的利息也更多。

这次加息后，IORB 已经从 3.65% 上调到 3.90%。钱的价格确实变贵了，但同时公共部门正在向银行和债券持有人支付更多利息，而这些钱最后很容易重新回到股票、债券、Crypto 这些资产里。

更关键的是银行体系本身还在扩表。

美联储 H.8 数据里，美国商业银行 Bank Credit 从 2025 年 8 月的约 18.67 万亿美元，涨到了今年 8 月的约 19.82 万亿美元。

贷款和租赁资产同期也从约 13.04 万亿涨到 14 万亿附近。

央行不一定疯狂印钱，但银行还在创造信用，所以“利率上涨”和“货币数量增加”完全可以同时发生。

所以高债务时代一个悖论：加息一边打击借钱的人，一边给拥有现金、国债和准备金的人发更多利息。

只要后面这条资金流足够大，紧缩就可能被部分对冲。

An experimental project that permanently writes an entire game's engine and data into an EVM chain in the form of contract bytecode. The goal is not just to make one game, but to build an on-chain game library using the same token and the same site. Next, they want to build the "first Online PVP on the blockchain."

The game program is packaged, chunked, and deployed as contract code. The browser reads the bytes from the chain using EXTCODECOPY. It verifies integrity using an on-chain verifiable keccak256 Merkle proof, and after confirmation, decompresses and compiles it into WebAssembly to run. The page itself hosts almost no game files; the game "lives inside the ledger."

Currently, there are two games using different engines, sharing the same on-chain read-and-verify system:

DEPTH: first-person maze

SIEGE: top-down arena shooter

The developer is Mart, whose X account is followed by Toly and Marc.

quoted_text:
我好像真的把 ChatGPT Pro 用到了大多数人碰不到的位置。

前段时间我发过一条：

自从学会用 ChatGPT Chat 的额度操控本地电脑以后，我会先把 Codex / Work 的周额度干完，然后继续用 Chat + MCPX 干活。

当时一直没撞到 Chat 上限，我甚至说：

“有一种 $200 无限用的感觉。”

今天终于撞到了。

而且撞完才发现，ChatGPT Pro 的额度结构比我原来理解的复杂得多。

我今天一直在真实干活，不是为了测额度故意刷。

同时开着很多长对话，用 Chat 做研究、调用工具、接 MCPX、操作本地任务、恢复 Session、执行和验证。

最后 GPT-5.6 的 Medium / High / Extra High 全部被我干到限额，三个档位现在都显示：

9 月 18 日 03:51 重置。

然后 Pro 也被我干到了限制：

9 月 19 日 11:11 重置。

我又去翻了 OpenAI 最新的官方文档，终于找到了一部分明确数字：

$200 Pro 的 GPT-5.6 Sol Pro：170 条 / 天。

GPT-5.6 Sol Pro + GPT-6 Pro 合计还有 200 条 / 天的限制。

GPT-6 Pro 另外还有 200 条 / 周。

至于 Medium / High / Extra High 这一组 GPT-5.6 Thinking，官方确认存在 Thinking limit，但目前没有公开具体容量。

最有意思的是：

这些都撞完以后，Instant 还活着。

我现在甚至还能继续用 Instant 处理刚才因为额度中断的任务。

所以我现在对 ChatGPT Pro 的理解彻底变了。

它不是简单的“$200 买多少条消息”。

更像是你手里有多种不同的计算资源和限额窗口。

我的实际使用路径现在已经变成：

Codex / Work → Chat 高推理 → Pro → Instant

一个地方撞墙，就把同一个任务和上下文 handoff 到仍然可用的执行面继续干。

过去一个月我基本就在干这件事：

把 AI 的“额度”，真正变成连续工作的计算资源。

以前我最好奇的是：

“ChatGPT Pro 到底能发多少条？”

现在我觉得更值得研究的问题是：

一个 $200/月的 ChatGPT Pro，在把这些资源全部利用起来以后，到底能换来多少真实完成的工作？

这可能才是 AI 订阅真正应该计算的 ROI。

text:
AI has made creating an app dramatically cheaper.

You can describe a product to Claude, Codex, or Cursor and have a working prototype before lunch.

BUT turning that prototype into a sovereign onchain product is still a completely different job.

You need consensus, validators, wallets, an explorer, security, liquidity, token infrastructure, and someone who knows how to connect everything without setting the building on fire.

That gap is where @CNPYNetwork fits.

Backed by @Arrington_Cap, @borderless_cap, @fenbushi, @snzholding, and others, Canopy is trying to become the singular stack for building an onchain app and launching it in one go.

Builders start with open-source templates, write in familiar languages, and use the AI coding tools they already know.

Instead of deploying another smart contract onto someone else’s blockspace, the product launches as a Nested Chain: an application-specific chain with its own logic, economics, and upgrade path.

Canopy then provides the validator network, shared security, wallet, explorer, and launch infrastructure. A new chain can borrow security from validators already bonding $CNPY rather than convincing an independent validator set to appear on day one.

If the app grows, it is not trapped forever.

It can remain under Canopy’s shared-security system or progressively move toward independent L1 operation.

Terminal adds the economic layer.

Creators can launch app tokens on a bonding curve, earn trading fees, then “graduate” into DEX liquidity and staking—while keeping chain ownership.

What each group gets:

- Builders: familiar languages, AI tools, no Solidity-first overhead, no DevOps/validator scramble
- Creators: bonding-curve launches, creator fees, DEX graduation, chain ownership
- Users: built-in wallet + explorer, token trading, possible app-token + CNPY staking rewards
- Stakers: one CNPY position can secure multiple Nested Chains and earn root + chain incentives
- Agents: APIs/templates designed for code-generating agents

➥ Why $CNPY matters

CNPY powers fees, secures validators, can be restaked across committees, and anchors Terminal launches + graduations.

Demand loop
- Terminal: launches/graduations drive CNPY velocity and staking after graduation
- Security: more chains → more committees → more CNPY bonded
- Usage: fees paid in CNPY recycle into rewards
- Builder flywheel: more apps → better examples for agents → faster launches

CEX/DEX listings help distribution, but access alone isn’t demand.

Canopy’s most interesting potential moat, however, may be its open-source flywheel. Every public application could expand a library of working examples for future coding agents.

--

➥ Final Thesis

More apps → smarter agents → shorter build cycles → even more apps and CNPY adoption.

That’s the core Canopy thesis, and it’s what ends up expressed in CNPY.

Not a ghost chain hoping developers show up someday, but an AI-first assembly line where the concept, the app, the chain, the security, and the token launch ship in one unbroken pipeline.

Now it comes down to this: can Canopy convert the hype into products people actually stick with?

text:
MCP 和 CLI 这场仗，我觉得从一开始就打错了地方。

先承认一件事：在协议的层面上，MCP 已经赢了。结构化 schema、OAuth、往上下文里直接回怼图片——这三样东西，CLI 想干都得自己撸一遍。Thariq 列的那些优势也属实，但注意，它们大多是客户端把以前的坑填完之后才冒出来的，不是协议天生送的。

不过有件事，MCP 在结构上做不到，CLI 生下来就会。

在数据进上下文之前，先削它一遍。

```bash
cat run.log | grep ERROR | tail -20
```

三个工具串成一根管子，最后进上下文的只有三行。换 MCP 来干同样的事，你得把整个 log 塞进 tool call 里，付 token，然后撞上长度上限。Rhys 在评论区提的本地文件就是这层意思——这不是"先后顺序"的问题，是结构的问题，根上的。

所以你现在能看懂那些做得好的 MCP server 到底在忙什么了。Tommy Long 说给工具加了个 jq 参数，Thariq 说让工具支持 query。翻译一下：每个 server 都在自己的 TypeScript 里，手写一遍 shell，手写一遍 grep，手写一遍 filter，再手写一遍分页。CLI 花了四十年把这个抽象磨完，MCP 现在从零再来一遍。

deferred tools 是同一个道理的另一面。CLI 的渐进式披露是白送的——`--help` 本来就是懒加载，没人需要为它写一行代码。MCP 得靠客户端额外再补一层出来。

所以准确的说法不是"模型工具调用变强了，所以 MCP 赢了"。是模型变强，再加上客户端把坑一个个补上，MCP 才勉强立得住。

而真正的瓶颈，从来不在协议，在客户端碎片化。

评论区那句"装了 MCP，也不知道有没有生效，要不要重启，坏了怎么 debug"——这才是大多数人的真实体验，不是 demo 里那种丝滑。CLI 的分发成本基本是零：谁都能写个二进制，任何 agent 都能跑。MCP 的分发成本，是客户端数量乘一遍集成。

我自己现在分得很简单：

跨权限边界的、要 OAuth 的、要被一堆 agent 复用的——MCP 赢，这个不用犹豫。

跑在同一台机器上、要跟文件和别的命令行工具串起来的——CLI 赢，而且短期内赢得很稳。

问题从来就不是哪个更好。问题是：这个集成，要不要活在我的文件系统里。

text:
AI 圈现在一个很大的问题，是我们都活在信息茧房里。

每天泡在 Twitter、Claude Code、Codex 里的人，会很自然地觉得 CLI 是未来，Agent 会吃掉 App，所有工作都应该自动化，最好一句话把电脑上的事全干完。

但你真去跟 AI 圈外的人聊，会发现完全是另一个世界。

大部分人不知道 CLI 是什么，也没有任何兴趣知道。

他们没有每天折腾 workflow，没有把 Gmail、日历、文档和浏览器全部接给 Agent，甚至还在用三年前就装好的那几个 App。

对很多普通人来说，AI 到今天最明确的价值依然很简单，比搜索好用一点，能问健康问题，买东西前帮忙参谋一下，偶尔写点东西。我身边不少同学在用的 AI 是豆包。

因为我们已经开始不用 App 了，所以 App 要死了；因为我们开始用 Agent 了，所以人人都会用 Agent。这其实是拿几万、几十万技术重度用户的生活，去脑补几十亿人的未来。

真正大的商业机会，反而可能没那么性感。

谁能把现在这些已经很强、但普通人根本懒得学的能力，做成一个不需要理解 Agent、不需要学 prompt、不需要知道 MCP 和 CLI 的产品，谁才有机会真正把 AI 往外推一层。

AI 圈最容易高估技术变化的速度，也最容易低估普通人改变习惯有多难。

而后者，可能比模型能力本身更值钱。

An extraordinary @Nature paper has just landed from the lab of @Sergiu_P_Pasca at @Stanford - led by Konstantin Kaganovsky. They have found a way to create "xenocortical mice" which have ~92% of their cortex occupied by a cortical organoid derived from human stem cells. This human-derived cortical graft integrates deeply with the host nervous system, supporting organised neural activity and behaviour.

This study is a milestone in synthetic biology and chimera research. It has the potential to generate multiple medical breakthroughs by providing an enhanced biological model of human brain tissue that allows behavioural as well as neural and genetic assays.

The Stanford team have been exceptionally thorough and proactive in addressing ethical concerns that comes from this frontier work. But their pioneering work  nonetheless raises many open questions: are the xenocortical mice conscious? Do they have any human-like properties of consciousness or cognition?  

@NitaFarahany and I will be addressing some of these questions in a forthcoming commentary - where we'll also offer an ethically-informed roadmap to guide this important research as it progresses. In this context, "pacing the frontier" really does make sense 😉

text: AI will prove your code is correct
author: vladtenev
quoted_text:
It's an increasingly common take that AI hacking means cybersecurity is doomed.

I disagree. I think cybersecurity is naturally defense-favoring once people get their shit together. And anyone who continues to hold cryptocurrency (including me, ~90% of my net worth) is implicitly making that bet.

Here's why I am making that bet.

First, the oversimplified punchy one-line statement:

If AI can prove Navier-Stokes and FLT, then AI can prove the statement "this program is secure" as a mathematical theorem. Even if the program is very complicated.

Now, the nuance:

(See also: https://t.co/6YPWgVT7rO )

The word "secure" is hiding all kinds of skeletons in the closet in terms of what it actually means. What does it mean for Signal (the encrypted messenger) to be "secure"?

The most basic definition you might think of is: no one who doesn't hold the recipient's secret key can read the contents of the message.

But:

* Did you remember to include _other_ critical forms of security? Can the adversary forge messages? Can the attacker prevent messages from reaching the recipient? Can they cause your client to crash by sending malformed messages?
* Have you made sure that your model of the adversary includes attackers that interfere with the protocol actively and not just passively? And attackers that interfere by replaying messages to you or the recipient that either of you sent over the wire at any point earlier?
* What if the adversary hacked (or _is_) the Signal server?
* How did you learn which public key belongs to the recipient in the first place? What if that process was tampered with?
* What if your device gets hacked at some point in the past or future - is your message still safe then?
* What if your key leaks because of a bug in your operating system? Or because you got a bugged version of the Signal client? Or what if the database is corrupted?
* Or the libraries, interpreter or compiler of the programming language you wrote it in?
* What if your key leaks because tiny perturbations in perceptible signals generated by the hardware leak mathematical relationships that can extract the key a few hundredths of a bit at a time?
* Are you hiding the *size* of the payload? Does that matter?
* You're definitely not hiding the identity of the sender and the recipient, and the exact time each message was sent (think: not just time-of-day, but also time deltas between one message and the next). Is that not enough to deduce a lot of important facts about what relationships you have, and what *kinds* of conversations you are having?

So ... even definitions can be over a thousand lines of code, and need deep careful thought to figure them out.

Working on making definitions more human-readable is of extreme importance - it's perhaps the only "high-level language" that matters right now.

But even still, even despite all of the above, for security-critical components, the definition is a much smaller attack surface than the implementation. Verifying that the definition is adequate is a much more tractable task than scanning over the code directly - and can become even more tractable with better tooling.

Definitions are also _additive_: if two groups have two different definitions A and B, then, well, you can just prove that the program satisfies both A and B. Code is not additive in this way: if a program is A + B, a bug in A _or_ B can sink the whole thing. Definitions are additive. And if you can't satisfy A and B at the same time, you've isolated the most important philosophical issue for your project to spend its next few weeks grappling with.

Sometimes, definitions are not much smaller than the implementation - UI components might be one example. But for many of the most critical components - message-passing protocols, sandboxes, cryptography like SNARKs and FHE - the asymmetry is real.

Historically, a large class of failures with this approach have come from people only verifying a small portion of their code, that they self-declared to be the security-critical portion, and ignoring the rest - and it turns out that something in the rest of the code is security-critical too.

This was reasonable back when verification was difficult and scarce. The solution today: sorry, you have to verify over literally your entire program, including database, networking, any caching layers, everything. Modern AI can do it.

So it's not about "the good guys find all the vulnerabilities before the bad guys do" - that could maybe work too, after all a finite program only has a finite number of vulns, but it's riskier - it's specifically an asymmetric strategy of making code that is much more resilient in the first place.

This is the kind of direction that Ethereum is going in for the next few years. There is no future for blockchains - especially blockchains with scalability and privacy - without doing this. We need to make software actually secure. And we have already made a lot of progress.

text:
Today in @Nature, we report a new approach to studying human brain development and modeling disease in vivo.

Human neural #assembloids and #organoids have opened new ways to study development in vitro, but they also have important limitations. Transplantation can provide a more physiological environment, yet human cortical cells then develop within a rodent brain that matures much faster, constraining their growth and integration. 

To address some of these limitations and obtain more advanced functional readouts relevant to disease biology, we generated #apallial mice, in which ~98% of the cortex and hippocampus fail to form, creating space for transplanted human cortical organoids to grow and integrate extensively. 

We call these #xenocortical mice (XCX).

Nearly 7 years in the making. Congratulations to an extraordinary team and wonderful collaborators!

text: “This is very core to Chinese strategic thinking (yes, Chan Chun Sing, as are most Singaporean leaders, is ethnically Chinese): the notion that legitimacy, not force, is the real currency of power.”
author: akshaybd
quoted_text:
I strongly encourage everyone to read the speech that Chan Chun Sing, Singapore's Defence Minister, just gave in Beijing: it's basically the polar opposite of a Hegseth speech - immensely wise and a refreshing proof that thoughtful statecraft still exists.

You can find the speech here: https://t.co/alGUQGK7J4  Below a summary of the best parts of the speech, in my opinion.

Much of the speech addresses the crucial question of the so-called "security dilemma", a key concept in international relations theory whereby one country's efforts to make itself safer almost inevitably make others feel less safe, triggering a spiral where everyone ends up more insecure.

As Chan Chun Sing puts it in his speech: "The true test of statecraft is this: how do we strengthen our own security without weakening the security of others, or without aggravating the insecurity of others?"

He says there are "three fundamental principles worth bearing in mind" in this regard, but that, first and foremost, it raises the question of "what 'winning' means": to him, defining "winning" as "outgunning or outlasting a rival" isn't sensible, it ought to be defined as winning others through the "power of our example", rather than "the example of our power."

It's extremely wise, when you think about it: do you actually "win" if you submit others by force, or do you merely prove that, for now, they simply lack the strength to resist? You've imposed your will, yes, but the principle you've imposed is that the strongest gets his way, and strength is expensive and it wanes.

Chan Chun Sing quotes Mencius, the classic Chinese philosopher, to illustrate this: "Power may compel others to comply. But in the end, it is trust that truly wins others over" (which is a trimmed version of the true original citation: "Those who subdue others by force do not win their hearts; they submit only because their own strength falls short. Those who subdue others by virtue win hearts that are glad and sincerely submissive, as the seventy disciples submitted to Confucius," 以力服人者，非心服也，力不赡也；以德服人者，中心悦而诚服也，如七十子之服孔子也。)

This is very core to Chinese strategic thinking (yes, Chan Chun Sing, as are most Singaporean leaders, is ethnically Chinese): the notion that legitimacy, not force, is the real currency of power. 

A state that has to coerce is following the "hegemonic way" (badao, 霸道) - which is brittle and unsustainable. The only sustainable long-term way to lead is the so-called "kingly way" (wangdao, 王道), where others follow you and emulate you voluntarily. Two concepts which incidentally come from Mencius too: "he who uses force while borrowing the name of benevolence is a hegemon (ba); he who practises benevolence through virtue is a true king (wang)."

Concretely, Chan Chun Sing say that states should pursue the following 3 principles to apply this in practice.

First of all, he points out that too many states "externalise domestic issues" as opposed to putting their own house in order. The idea being that a leadership confident at home doesn't need foreign enemies to hold itself together, and can therefore act in its "enlightened long-term interest" abroad. Whereby an insecure one uses foreign policy "for political gain."

No prizes for guessing what country he is referring to here...

The second principle is that "interdependence breeds stability" as opposed to being "a source of vulnerability." 

Which makes sense: mutual exposure turns competitors into stakeholders in each other's stability. Cut exposure in the name of "resilience" or "de-risking" and, really, the only thing you've achieved is to make confrontation and conflict cheaper.

Lastly, and this is perhaps the most important principle: "first, do no harm."

Chan Chun Sing again quotes famous Chinese sayings: "turn big problems into small ones, and small ones into nothing" (大事化小，小事化了), which is what happens when there's trust between states, versus "turn small problems into big ones, and make trouble out of nothing" (小事化大，无事生非), which is what happens when there isn't.

The idea is that every unnecessary provocation, every "freedom of navigation" stunt, every gratuitous sanction is a withdrawal from a trust account that is very expensive to fill and, as he says, can be emptied "in a single instant."

Chan Chun Sing ends his speech on what being a “responsible major country” - a key concept in contemporary Chinese international relations - means, and how, "the more responsible major powers are, the less concerned small countries will be."

Besides the above three fundamental principles, he says that "strategic patience" is also crucial, defined as: "Not every capability needs to be advertised; not every advantage needs to be immediately pressed; and not every provocation demands an immediate response."

In other words, true confidence doesn't need to prove itself and restraint is a form of strength: a great power that feels compelled to respond to everything is, in effect, letting its rivals set its agenda. And whoever needs to constantly show force is in fact projecting its own fear that without the show, nobody would believe it. 

As Margaret Thatcher once brilliantly put it (I hate to quote her but this is too good): "Being powerful is like being a lady. If you have to tell people you are, you aren't."

That's it, if you want the rest, I truly encourage you to read the full speech: pure undistilled wisdom, from a man who runs the defence of a country smaller than Los Angeles and obviously understands power far better than the man in charge of the largest military on earth. Which is its own form of tragedy.

Coding Agent 上，MCP 像已经死了。但是 @trq212 却说：多数集成里，MCP 已经比 CLI 更好用了，似乎有点矛盾？

如果平时基本只用 Agent 写代码，观感会非常统一，git、gh、docker、ffmpeg...直接用CLI来操作多美好，如果挂一层 GitHub MCP、Filesystem MCP，不仅慢，而且 token 占用和消耗还很多，甚至还多了一个后台进程。 

但把场景换掉，结论就会有质的变化：

CLI 不能来做 Figma 画布任务，但是 MCP 可以；Sentry、Stripe、Notion、Linear 更想基于账户的 OAuth，而不是把 API key 塞进 Agent，MCP的服务端可以支持；ChatGPT、Claude的云端会话里根本没有 shell，CLI 无处运行，但是 MCP 可以运行在企业的服务器上；此外，如果企业要审批、审计、跨客户端复用时，MCP天然比 curl 更能支持这些场景。

总之，本地、高频、已有好 CLI 的，继续用命令行； 没有对象模型、没有鉴权、没有终端的，MCP 仍然是更干净的那根线。

text:
Manus 从 Meta 手里被拆回来几个月，估值反而要翻倍了。

Bloomberg 最新消息，Manus 正在谈一轮约 5 亿美元融资，目标估值 40 亿美元，目前已经接近完成。

Meta 去年花大约 20 亿美元收购 Manus，后来中国监管要求交易撤回。Manus 创始团队、腾讯、HSG 和真格等老股东，最后又按差不多 20 亿美元的价格把股份买了回来。

现在转头融资，价格已经到了 40 亿美元。

Meta 收购时 Manus 年化收入大概 1 亿美元，到今年 6 月已经被报道做到 4～5 亿美元。如果这个数字没有明显缩水，40 亿美元差不多是 8～10 倍年化收入，对今天的 AI 公司甚至谈不上特别夸张。

Manus 自己不训练基础模型，但照样可以靠产品、Agent workflow 和分发做到几十亿美元估值。过去大家总觉得应用层会被模型吃掉，Manus 至少暂时证明了，中间这层还有很大的钱可以赚。

当然它的问题也越来越明显。

Claude、Kimi 这些基础模型正在快速补 Computer Use 和桌面 Agent，单纯「AI 能替我操作电脑」这件事，很难永远成为护城河。

UsePaid is a project that automatically converts on-chain token creator fees into USD and sends them to X users’ accounts.

When a user launches a token on Pump, they direct all creator fees to the project’s treasury and include an X account in the token description. 80% of the fees generated by that token are then paid to that X account in USD through X Money, while the remaining 20% is used to buy back and burn PAID.

Once the USD accumulates, the system pays it out in batches based on the total amount. Common thresholds are $5, $10, $20, $50, $100, $250, $500, and $1,000, with payments made every time another $1,000 threshold is reached afterward.

The recipient does not need to register in advance. X Money sends the payment directly to the account. If the recipient has not enabled X Money, the funds are held for a period of time. If they are not claimed before expiration, the funds are returned and used to buy back PAID.

PAID is the protocol’s value-capture token. Its sole function is to be continuously bought back and burned using that 20% of fees. The more fees generated, the more PAID is removed from circulation.

PAID’s own trading fees all go to the protocol treasury and are not included in the 80/20 split.

Currently, 1% of the total supply has already been burned.

머니플로우 '26.9.17 

연준: 3년 만에 올릴게
SK하이닉스, 삼성전자: 열심히 스쿼트할게
조선, 방산: 오늘은 내가 주도할게
AI인프라: 아직은 현역으로 뛸게

FOMC에서 연준이 드디어 3년만에 기준금리 인상을 발표함.
몇주 내내 금리인상 기정사실화자고 했던게 드디어 현실화됨.
나스닥은 -0.01%로 보합. SOX는 0.63%오르며 오히려 상승.

워시는 물가가 높다 말하지만 정작 점도표는 비둘기적이었음.
물가는 결국 유가 영향도 크니까 아직 맘놓고 안심하긴 이름.
그래도 FOMC 이벤트가 우려했던것 대비 스무스하게 지나감.

트럼프가 후티와 비밀회담했다는 뉴스 덕에 유가도 좀 내려옴.
WTI는 -3.2%하락 $102로 마감. $100위 인데도 안도하게됨.

국장도 NXT에서는 IT 위주로 반등 시작하더니 차익실현 나옴.
코스피 갭상승 반납하고 약보합까지 밀려버린 상태(힘내임마)
코스닥은 그래도 0.5% 상승하며 상대적으로 잘 버티는 중.

삼성전자 -0.3%, SK하이닉스 -1.1%까지 잘 오르다 밀려버림.
SOX가 올라도 메모리는 약하더니 국장까지 데려가주진 않음.
아침에 올려놓고 점심에 빼는 짜장면 장세는 좀 골때리긴 함.

오늘 구원 투수로 나선 것은 산업재. 그 중에서도 조선,  방산.

HD현대중공업, 삼성중공업 7% 안팎으로 급등하는 모습.
미 전쟁부 부차관보가 한화오션 방문하며 마스가 기대감 붙음.
한화시스템도 10%넘게 오르며 방산 섹터를 이끌고 있음.
UAE 에지그룹과 통합대공망 구축 JV설립 조회공시가 나옴.
트럼프-후티 비밀회담 결과로 사우디 안도와주니 더 급등.

금융주도 오르지만 전부 동반상승하는 그림은 아님. 
보험주는 추가 금리인상 기대감 약화로 오히려 빠지는 모습.

반도체가 약하다고 AI 관련주나 IT가 다 약세인건 아님.
AI DC 투자 관련주 지엔씨에너지 8%, 이수페타시스 5% 상승
속도조절 노이즈로 싸잡혔지만 그 안에서도 반응이 갈림.

원전 테마도 산업재 동반 상승하며 두산에너빌리티 2% 상승.
대미투자 협상이 엎어진건 아님. 22일로 미뤄졌으니 재료연장
MOU 서명하는 날까지는 아직 재료가 살아있다고 봐줘야함.

시장은 꼬물거리는데 상승, 하락 종목 수는 그래도 엇비슷 함.
양시장 모두 각 시장에서는 상승 종목 수가 더 많은 상황.
오르다 밀린게 좀 짜치긴 하지만 어떻게보면 배부른 소리임.
금리 인상했는데 급락안하고 잘 버티는게 감지덕지 일수도

FOMC라는 큰 고비 하나 넘겼지만 바로 꽃길이 열리진않는 듯
내일은 미국 선옵만기 네마녀의 날. 그리고 다음주부턴 연휴.
일본은 월화수 3일 연휴. 한국은 목부터 연휴라 3일만 열림.
연휴를 앞두고 적극적인 매수세는 눈치보일 수도 있는 상황.

이제 유가만 잠잠해지면 한숨 돌리지 않을까 싶은 상황임. 
다만 전쟁 상황은 예측이 안되니까 여전히 안심할 수는 없음.
여전히 시장 좀 반등했다고 마음놓고 따라붙긴 애매한 시장.

오늘 완만한 상승 기대했는데 내 생각보다 덜커덩거리고 있음.
그래도 난 금리 인상 여파가 스무스하게 넘어가고있다 생각함.

조선, 방산은 낙폭과대에서 순환매 도는 느낌.
스페이스X 궤도비행 뉴스로 우주 테마까지 급등하고 있음.
시장이 확실히 꿈틀꿈틀 준비하는것 같아서 그나마 긍정적.

다들 어제 금리 인상 이후 오늘 시장 어떻게 느끼는지 궁금함.
그래도 생각했던것보단 스무스한거 같지 않음?

p,s. '~게'시리즈 요약 -> 프리마켓 머니플로우 -> 머니플로우
그리고 밤에는 클로징 코멘트. 주말엔 주간일정, 다음주 전략.
이 컨텐츠들은 정기적으로 작성중이니 챙겨보시기 바람.
